title: Aging hearts and vessels: Masters of adaptation and survival
abstract: Aging has become one of the most critical issues for industrialised nations, because population average age, and thus the incidence of age-associated disease, has markedly risen to create a major burden as patients draw heavily on the need for continuing medical treatment and hospital and other community services. Despite major advances in medicine in recent years, cardiovascular disease remains the greatest cause of morbidity and mortality. Age, per se, confers the major risk for cardiovascular disease because specific pathophysiological mechanisms that underlie these diseases become superimposed on cardiac and vascular substrates that have been modified by the “aging process” [1–3]. In healthy humans rigorously screened to exclude cardiovascular disease, non-human primates, and rodents, the large elastic arteries become dilated and stiffen and the intima thickens and exhibits cellular and sub-cellular features that resemble those that occur during vascular inflammation and injury [1]. Age-associated changes in cardiac structure (increased left ventricular myocyte size, reduced myocyte number, increased extracellular matrix remodelling, fibrosis) and resting function (reduced early diastolic filling) occur, in part, in response to aging of the arterial system [2]. Cardiovascular reserve function in advanced aged without cardiovascular disease is limited by suboptimal ventricular–vascular coupling due to an age-associated augmentation of vascular afterload and reduced myocardial contractility due, in part, to a diminished effectiveness of β-adrenergic modulation [3,4]. Senescent cardiac myocytes are characterized by altered metabolic, ionic, and electrical properties due partly to increased myocyte size, altered membrane composition, reduced capacity to maintain ion homeostasis, reduced Ca2+ tolerance, increased reactive O2 species levels in response to a variety of stressors, and reduced adaptive capacity to invoke “ischemic preconditioning-like” intracellular signal transduction for post-stress survival [5–9]. Age-targeted therapies such as those involving diet, exercise habits, gene therapy, or pharmacological agents that interfere with or beneficially regulate angiotensin II and other hormones, epigenetic factors, collagen cross-linking, metalloprotease regulation, inflammation, endogenous antioxidant systems, and mitochondria, are thus required to prevent or delay the structural and functional changes that accompany age-associated cardiovascular functional decline and the risk for disease [10–15]. However, the remarkable resilience and adaptive capacity of the heart and cardiovascular system to meet the rigorous and diverse demands of our ‘longer’ lives also offer us great opportunity to unravel nature's molecular fabric. Some of these themes have been treated in reviews or original articles that delineate new insights into the mechanisms underpinning cardiovascular aging in this Spotlight Issue of Cardiovascular Research dedicated to Cardiovascular Aging. This challenging issue features 12 reviews and 11 original articles that tackle cardiovascular aging at the level of the genome, myocardial metabolism and function, and the vasculature. Volkova et al. [16] review cardiac transcriptome analysis techniques and their significance to determine pathways, regulatory sequences, and candidate genes implicated in aging and ultimately to identify genetic causes of aging in humans. Park and Prolla [17] review differential gene expression patterns determined via gene array analysis of mouse heart, brain, and skeletal muscle and caloric restriction, a dietary model that retards aging. Age-associated transcriptional patterns of genes required for energy metabolism resemble those patterns apparent with the development of cardiac hypertrophy. Caloric restriction effectively blocks these age-associated changes in gene expression whereas antioxidant diet with Coenzyme Q10 or alphalipoic acid does not, producing modest impact on expression; thus, it is proposed that oxidative stress contributes, but may not be causal, to cardiac aging. Edo and Andrés [18] review the potential role of telomeres and telomere-related proteins in aging and, in particular, present studies that indicate that telomere integrity is eroded with age and that the reduction in telomere length (in smooth muscle, endothelial, and white blood cells) is a primary factor predisposing vascular tissue to atherosclerosis and the reduced capacity for neovascularisation. This exhaustion of telomere length is most prominent under conditions of high oxidative stress, but particularly in hypertensives, diabetics, and those with coronary artery disease. It is proposed that induction of increased human telomerase reverse transcriptase expression in progenitor cells or via transfection may offer post-infarct novel therapy for revascularisation. With regard to potential genomic therapies for treating age-related decline in cardiac function, Schmidt et al. [19] present original data that demonstrate that gene transfer of parvalbumin for its overexpression in Fischer 344 rats improves myocardial calcium handling and diastolic function in aging without augmenting energy consumption. In addition, Speer et al. [20], demonstrate that vascular calcification due to reduced cellular expression of osteopontin can also be targeted by a gene-transfer approach. Using a ‘knockout’ transgenic mouse model of osteopontin, these authors use retroviral transduction of osteopontin cDNA to rescue osteopontin−/− aortic smooth muscle cells from inorganic phosphate-induced calcification. The delineation of the mitochondrial role in aging and in myocardial cell adaptation and survival in disease is highly controversial. In two reviews with differing emphases, Di Lisa and Bernardi [21] and Juhaszova et al. [22] update for us the role of mitochondrial permeability transition and the regulatory signalling that modulates mitochondrial capacity in cardioprotection. Willems et al. [23] appraise the regulatory role of endogenous adenosine in cardioprotection against ischemic stress and the impact of an age-associated decline in adenosine-dependent cardioprotective signal transduction mechanisms. Although endogenous release of parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP; present in vascular smooth muscle, endothelial, and atrial myocardial cells) has been shown to contribute to protection of the isolated rat heart against ischemia-reperfusion injury in young adults, PTHrP has paradoxically opposite effects in aged or hypertrophied isolated rat hearts (Wistar and SHR) [24]. Ross and Schlüter [24] demonstrate that the reduced capacity for post-ischemic contractile recovery evident in aged or hypertrophied hearts from SHR can be abrogated by use of a cardiac-specific PTHrP antagonist delivered just prior to ischemia, and these authors propose that PTHrP post-receptor coupling is modified during aging independently of pressure-induced hypertrophy. Kaye and Esler [25] review how the progressive, age-related changes in the human subcortical forebrain and the sympathetic nervous system that lead to increased norepinephrine ‘spillover’, reduced clearance of plasma catecholamines, and reduced neural reuptake of catecholamines may be important causal factors predisposing for essential hypertension, cardiac failure, and ventricular arrhythmias. Later in this issue, Vonend et al. [26] present an original study examining the renovascular effects of neuropeptide Y and ATP, which are co-transmitted with noradrenaline in sympathetic neurons that are overactive in hypertension. The theme of age-associated remodelling is extended further to the atrial myocardium in an original study by Anyukhovsky and colleagues [27] in which they examine the induction of arrhythmogenesis in a canine model of rapid atrial pacing. Atrial fibrillation is the most common chronic arrhythmia responsible for an overwhelming burden of morbidities and continuing medical care. Atrial fibrillation is closely associated with increased age and remodelling of cellular electrical properties, extracellular matrix, and fibrosis. A significant proportion of this spotlight issue on cardiovascular aging is focused on inflammatory signalling. Kritchevsky et al. [28] review the expression of C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, IL-6, IL10, and TNFα in aging and the predisposition for coronary heart disease and stroke. Yamamoto and colleagues [29] review the role of elevated plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 with aging and the increased risk for thrombogenesis and inflammation. The importance of elevated inflammatory markers as risk factors for cardiovascular disease is also addressed in the original article by Deten et al. [30], who examine the role of IL-6 and IL-1b in aging and in the development of myocardial infarction. The important role of endothelial remodelling in aging and the decline in endothelium-dependent regulation of vasodilation is reviewed by Brandes et al. [31]. They highlight this decline as being due partly to increased superoxide and peroxynitrite formation, diminished eNOS, estrogens, and dehydroepiandosterone, and the increased inflammatory signalling that promotes iNOS. Dubey et al. [32] review the vascular consequences of menopause and relevance of estrogen therapy. Shipley and Muller-Delp [33] present experimental data that shows aging of Fischer 344 rats decreases the endothelium-dependant responsiveness of coronary arterioles to endothelin, potassium chloride, and pressure-induced myogenic responses. In an original study of the effects of endothelin-1 on constrictor responses in Fischer 344 rat coronary arteries, Korzick et al. [34] examine the age-associated increase in coronary resistance and dysfunctional PKC-mediated signal transduction due to increased Ca2+-sensitive PKCα, -βI, and -βII. Although Donato et al. [35] report an age-associated increase in gastrocnemius arteriole vasoconstrictor responsiveness and sensitivity to endothelin-1, they were unable to demonstrate that exercise training could reverse the age-associated effects of vasoconstrictor responsiveness to endothelin-1. Vascular remodelling in aging is also emphasised in the review by Dao et al. [36] on the age-associated increase in large artery stiffness and resultant loss of capacitance and faster pulse wave velocity. The underlying vascular remodelling that ultimately predisposes for hypertension includes loss of smooth muscle cells and elasticity coupled with medial calcification and accumulation of advanced glycation end-products in collagen and elastin. The impact of age-associated remodelling of the extracellular matrix, under the regulation of metalloproteinases, is examined in original studies by Defawe et al. [37] and Lindsey et al. [38]. As progress is made in further elucidating the diverse molecular mechanisms that underlie the cardiovascular alterations that accompany advancing age, novel therapies must emerge that will specifically retard or reverse “unsuccessful” cardiovascular aging [15]. The possibility of identifying factors that modify cardiovascular changes [2,9–11], including lifestyle factors, is reinforced by the substantial variability among older persons in the degree to which these cardiovascular changes that accompany aging occur. Treatments targeting structural factors have begun. ALT-711, a novel thiazolium agent that breaks non-enzymatic cross-links between glucose and amino groups that generate advanced glycation end-products with increasing age, reduces cardiac and arterial stiffness both in non-human primates [12] and in humans [13]. Chronic inhibition of angiotensin receptor signalling also substantially retards the age-associated increase in collagen content and intimal-medial thickening and stiffening in rodents [3]. Dietary interventions can modulate cardiovascular properties [5–7,17]. Food fat content has been shown to adversely affect vascular stiffness and endothelial function, and diets that are reduced in sodium are associated with reduced arterial stiffening with aging, independent of their blood pressure-lowering effects [13]. While such preventive lifestyle or pharmacological strategies may be explored even now, future genetic characterization of individuals will likely allow person-specific stratification with respect to risk, efficacy, and cost effectiveness of measures to retard vascular aging in order to reduce cardiovascular functional disability and disease at older ages.

title: Cancer and epigenetics – basic research and clinical implications: Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion Foundation, October 2004
abstract: The Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar (HCS) and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion (TBP) Foundation was held on 30–31 October 2004 at the International Conference Center, Hiroshima. The symposium consisted of 12 special lectures and 34 free paper presentations for poster session; approximately 250 people were present and actively discussed topics relating to cancer and epigenetics, from basic research to clinical implication. Prior to this symposium, an Open Lecture to the public by HCS was held on 30 October. Kazunori Kodama (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima) spoke about cancer prevention to more than 120 people. To begin the meeting, Eiichi Tahara (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima), Chairman of the HCS Foundation, gave an opening address. Tahara introduced a brief background and the purpose of this series of symposia. Since the establishment of the HCS Foundation in 1992, annual international symposia are organized to create an opportunity for basic scientists and clinical researchers to exchange ideas for cancer research, cancer prevention and cancer therapy. This year, the organizing committee planned to explore the important issue of ‘Cancer and Epigenetics’. The epigenetic mechanism is deeply involved in the pathogenesis of human cancers. CpG island methylator phenotypes (CIMP) might be one of the major pathways responsible for the development of gastrointestinal cancer. Because inactivation of various suppressor genes by promoter methylation or chromatin modification commonly occurs in human cancers, these may provide potential targets for therapeutic intervention. The participants profit by exchanging and learning ideas from informative presentations and discussions, and also contribute to future development in cancer treatment and prevention. Jean-Pierre Issa (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) delivered a lecture, entitled ‘Bedside epigenetics’, and described the impact of epigenetic process in tumorigenesis and cancer management. Epigenetic changes in cancer consist of primary DNA methylation changes, as well as histone code changes related to DNA methylation or abnormalities in specific histone modifying enzymes. The field is rapidly moving towards clinical applications in patients with cancer, including risk assessment, early detection, prognostication and therapeutic targeting. In colorectal cancer, methylation in normal appearing mucosa appears to increase with age and to be particularly pronounced in patients with advanced preneoplastic and neoplastic lesions. Measurement of methylation in normal appearing mucosa could therefore predict the risk of cancer development, as will be argued for the MGMT gene. In multiple tumor types, a high degree of CIMP appears to be associated with a poor prognosis following standard management. In colorectal cancer, the presence of CIMP in patients who present with stage IV disease is associated with a short survival following 5-fluorouracil based therapy. Drugs that inhibit DNA methylation (5-azacytidine and 5-aza-2’-deoxycytidine, or DAC) are now used in clinical trials for various malignancies. Data suggest that, in myeloid malignancies, the efficacy of DAC is greater at low doses that favor hypomethylation over cytotoxicity, and that responses require the induction of in-vivo hypomethylation. Overall, it seems clear that epigenetic processes will have a significant and varied impact on the management of neoplasia in humans. Mitsuo Oshimura (Tottori University, Yonago) described the epigenetic regulation in imprinted domains in cancer. Genomic imprinting, the phenomenon whereby mono-allelic expression of certain genes occurs depending on their parental origin, plays an important role in mammalian development, growth and cell differentiation. Disturbance of normal imprinting is frequently associated with various types of cancer. LIT1 is an imprinting control center at human chromosome 11p15.5. Several lines of evidence suggested that LIT1 transcript regulates chromatin modifications, resulting in alteration of gene expression in the domain in some, but not all cancer cells. The human paternally expressed gene 3 (PEG3) on chromosome 19q13.4 is one of the candidate tumor suppressor genes for glioma. It has been identified that three expressed sequence tags (EST), H80201, H78825 and AW197312, exhibit paternal allele-specific expression, using human monochromosomal hybrids containing a paternal or maternal origin of PEG3 locus. The EST H80201 was expressed only from the paternal allele in normal lymphoblasts by using a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). Monoallelic expression of EST H80201 was also detected in non-tumor adult brain tissues of gliomas. These EST were located directly adjacent to PEG3 in a head-to-head orientation. This new transcript, imprinted transcript 1, is located upstream but oriented opposite to PEG3 (ITUP1). Bisulfite sequencing and reverse transcription (RT)-PCR indicated that hypermethylation of the promoter correlated with the absence of these transcripts. ITUP1 and PEG3 may be coordinately regulated, and down-regulation of both genes could be important in the development of glioma. Hidenobu Soejima (Saga University, Saga) presented on the epigenetic regulation of LIT1 imprinting domain and its implication in human diseases. To clarify the chromatin-based imprinting mechanism, the histone modification status at a differentially CpG methylated region of LIT1 (DMR-LIT1) was investigated. Mice harboring targeted deletion of DMR-LIT1 on the paternally inherited chromosome and microcell hybrids harboring targeted deletion of human DMR-LIT1 resulted in the de-repression of imprinted genes including KIP2, indicating that DMR-LIT1 is an imprinting control region for the domain. This region is demethylated in half Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) patients and in several tumors. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays revealed that in both species, DMR-LIT1 with the CpG-methylated, maternally derived inactive allele showed histone H3 Lys9 (H3K9) methylation, whereas the CpG unmethylated, paternally active allele was acetylated on histone H3/H4 and methylated on H3 Lys4 (H3K4). In the BWS patients with DMR-LIT1 imprinting defect, H3K9 methylation disappeared completely. Furthermore, in esophageal cancer cell lines, expression of imprinted KIP2 gene was statistically correlated with loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1, not with KIP2 promoter methylation itself. Loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1 was also associated with loss of H3K9 methylation. These findings suggest that the histone modification at DMR-LIT1 plays an important role in imprinting control within the imprinting domain, and that loss of histone H3K9 methylation together with CpG demethylation on the maternal allele might lead to the BWS phenotype and might be involved in esophageal cancer. Satoshi Fujii (Hiroshima Red-Cross Hospital, Hiroshima) described the role of histone modification in the imprinted tumor suppressor gene. ARHI is a maternally imprinted tumor suppressor gene whose expression from the paternal allele is markedly down-regulated in breast cancer in addition to loss of heterozygosity. Consistent with imprinting, all three CpG islands of ARHI gene were partially methylated in normal human breast epithelial cells. Reactivation of ARHI expression in breast cancer cell lines by CpG demethylating agents and/or histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors was related to the methylation status of the CpG islands in the ARHI promoter, especially CpG island II. ChIP assays revealed that treatment with a CpG demethylating agent and/or HDAC inhibitor could increase ARHI expression in breast cancer cells, with a corresponding increase in histone H3K9/18 acetylation and decrease H3K9 methylation. The similar experiments were performed in mouse A9 hybrid cell lines containing only a single maternal (A9–1M) or paternal (A9–1P) allele of human chromosome 1. The histone H3K9/18 acetylation level at ARHI was much higher in A9–1P cells than in A9–1M cells. By contrast, A9–1M cells had much higher H3K9 methylation levels at ARHI than did A9–1P cells. Only treatment with a combination of HDAC inhibitor and a demethylating agent reactivated the imprinted allele. These data suggest that parental allele-specific DNA methylation, histone H3 acetylation and H3K9 methylation are key regulatory mechanisms in ARHI imprinting. Yutaka Kondo (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) gave a talk on the role of histone modifications in tumor suppressor genes in cancers. The status of histone modification at silenced tumor suppressor gene loci was examined in colorectal cancers. DNA methylation and histone modifications (H3K4 undermethylation, H3K9 underacetylation and H3K9 hypermethylation) were closely correlated at silenced loci in colorectal cancers. Treating cells with inhibitors of HDAC and inhibitors of DNA methylation resulted in large effects on the histone code associated with reactivation of gene expression, suggesting that the sequence of loss of histone acetylation followed by gain of histone methylation on H3K9 is needed for silencing. Next, to evaluate the global distribution of target genes silenced by H3K9 methylation in cancer, a human CpG island microarray was probed with DNA obtained by ChIP using anti H3K9 methylated antibody or anti H3K9 acetylated antibody. Eleven genes, one EST, two unknown fragments and 13 repetitive sequences were identified as targets of H3K9 modification. In addition, a strong correlation was found between the ratio of K9 methylation/acetylation and DNA methylation in those clones. To examine the mechanisms of aberrant histone methylation and which histone methyltransferases may be involved, RNAi-based inhibition of histone methyltransferase, SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 expression was studied. The preliminary data show that treatment of cancer cells with RNAi to SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 potentiates gene reactivation, markedly inhibits cell growth and causes profound morphological changes in cancer cells. Mitsuyoshi Nakao (Kumamoto University, Kumamoto) described the role of methylated DNA-binding proteins in transcription and genomic stability. DNA methylation contributes to genome regulation including control of gene expression and chromatin structure. Genome stability is also linked to this epigenetic modification. In the nucleus, the methylated DNA is recognized by methylated DNA-binding domain (MBD) proteins. There are at least five mammalian MBD proteins: MeCP2, MBD1, MBD2, and MBD3 for transcriptional repression, and MBD4 (also known as MED1) for mismatch repair as a thymine glycosylase. Among them, MBD1 acts as a transcriptional regulator through the cooperation of MBD, cysteine-rich CXXC domains, and a C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD). The MBD of MBD1 recruits histone methyltransferase Suv39h1, HDAC1/HDAC2 and HP1 that can bind methyl H3K9. MBD1-containing chromatin-associated factor 1 (MCAF1), also known as the human homolog of murine ATFa-associated modulator (AM), interacts with TRD of MBD1. It is particularly noted that MCAF1/AM converts dimethyl to trimethyl H3K9 by histone methyltransferase SETDB1/ESET. These data indicate that MBD1 may tether Suv39h1-HP1 and SETDB1-MCAF1 complexes to methylated DNA regions, suggesting the presence of pathways from DNA methylation to histone methylation for epigenetic regulation. Furthermore, MBD1 is involved in genome integrity by cooperating with methyl-purine DNA glycosylase, one of the key molecules in the base excision repair. Issay Kitabayashi (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) reported the function and regulation of the AML1 transcription factor complex. Specific chromosome translocations are frequently found in human leukemia and often result in the expression of fusion gene products. The genes encoding the AML1/CBF transcription factor complex are the most frequent targets of these translocations. The AML1 complex contains histone acetyltransferases such as p300 and MOZ, promyelocytic leukemia (PML), a corepressor mSIN3A and a protein kinase (AML1K). MOZ and p300/CBP stimulates AML1-dependent transcription. In contrast, a leukemia-associated fusion MOZ-CBP inhibited AML1-mediated transcription and inhibits differentiation of M1 myeloid cells. A specific isoform of PML (PML I) was able to recruit AML1 and coactivator p300 in PML nuclear bodies and enhance the AML1-mediated transcription in the presence of p300. Overexpression of PML I stimulated myeloid cells to differentiate into neutrophils. These results suggest that PML I could act as a mediator for AML1 and its coactivator p300/CBP to assemble into functional complexes, and consequently, activate AML1-dependent transcription and myeloid cell differentiation. AML1K mediated phosphorylation of AML1, p300 and MOZ. AML1K stimulated HAT activity of p300 and transcription activation by GAL4-p300. AML1K strengthened interaction between AML1 and MOZ. The genes encoding AML1 and some of the AML1-interacting proteins are the targets of leukemia-associated chromosome translocations, suggesting that common pathways may be shared by distinct myeloid malignancies and underscores the importance of this complex in hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis. Toshikazu Ushijima (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) focused on genome-wide screening techniques for differences in DNA methylation between two genomes. His group previously developed methylation-sensitive-representational difference analysis (MS-RDA). The advantage of MS-RDA is that it focuses on unmethylated and CpG-rich regions of the genome, and thus differential methylation of unique CpG islands can be intensively screened, avoiding interference by repetitive sequences. In an analysis of human stomach cancer, they identified silencing of nine genes, Lysyl oxidase (LOX), H-ras like suppressor (HRASLS), bA305P22.2.3, Filamin-c (FLNc/g-filamin/ABPL), HAND1, a homolog of RIKEN2210016F16, FLJ32130, Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor g angiopoietin-related (PGAR/HFARP/ANGPTL4/ARP4) and Thrombomodulin (TM), as a result of methylation of 5′-CpG islands. Among the nine genes, growth-suppressive activities had been reported for LOX and HRASLS in ras-transformed fibroblasts and for TM in melanoma cells. Tumor-suppressive activities of LOX and HRASLS were examined in gastric cancers by introducing their cDNA into gastric cancer cell lines. Introduction of LOX successfully suppressed cellular growth, colony formation in soft agar, and tumor growth in nude mice, while that of HRASLS did not. These results indicate that LOX is a novel tumor-suppressor gene in human gastric cancers. The power of methylation-based genome-wide screening was impressive. Victor V. Lobanenkov (National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, USA) presented epigenetic regulation of human genome universally involving CTCT/BORIS-binding regions. Many human pathologies including cancer and imprinting disorders may involve common types of epigenetic deregulations non-randomly distributed throughout genomes. It is hypothesized that an ‘epigenetic havoc’ often observed in such pathologies, including LOI in tumors that exhibit regional genome-wide demethylation with a narrower site-specific hypermethylation, might be associated with a common particular malfunction of the DNA-targeting mechanisms necessary for the proper localization and functional reading of epigenetic marks. Such targeting should involve sequence-specific DNA-binding factors, but their identity remained elusive until CTCF-binding regions have emerged as the most likely places of epigenetic modifications in mammals. The duplicated ‘multivalent’ 11 Zn-finger DNA-binding domains (11ZF-DBD), which comprise one-third of the total length in the two paralogous nuclear factors of similar size, CTCF and BORIS, appear to conduct the DNA-targeting part in the molecular orchestra of normal and aberrant epigenetic marking in mammals. Unlike normal somatic cells with CTCF, the vast majority of cancer cells are found to abnormally coexpress CTCF and BORIS together. Several studies of the IGF2/H19 LOI, caused by altering normally mono-allelic CTCF-binding in tumors by aberrant bi-allelic hypo- or hyper-methylation of at least one of several CTCF-sites in the H19 ICR, suggested that CTCF and its targets are taking the central stage in human cancer (epi)genetics. An ongoing mapping of the 11ZF-DBD-binding sites with gel-shifts and verifying each novel site for methylation-sensitive CTCF versus BORIS binding in vivo, strongly supports an idea that misdirected epigenetic regulation in already developed tumors is mediated through a misuse of varying sequences recognized by the 11ZF-DBD. Hidetoshi Tahara (Hiroshima University, Hiroshima) gave a talk on genetic and epigenetic regulation of cell cycle genes in human aging. Cellular senescence causes cells to arrest proliferation, essentially irreversibly, by induction of cyclin dependent kinase inhibitors such as p16INK4a and p21waf1. Loss of telomeric repeat DNA during cell proliferation also leads to cellular senescence. Ectopic expression of the catalytic subunit of the telomerase gene, hTERT, resulted in elongation of telomere and extended cell division number. The hTERT gene was introduced into many types of normal human cells to established immortalized cells with normal characteristics. In contrast, in epithelial cells, all hTERT immortalized cells do not have significant levels of p16, but p21 expression is down-regulated by hTERT under telomere length dependent manner. Promoter methylation of p16 was found in all of hTERT immortalized epithelial cells. Epigenetic alteration such as p16 promoter methylation is necessary for cellular immortalization in human epithelial cells. title: Synopsis: 2005 Annual Meeting of the American Society of Andrology
abstract: The 30th Annual Meeting of the American Society of Andrology (ASA) was held in Seattle, Wash, April 2–4, 2005. The Annual Meeting was preceded by the Testis Workshop, held from March 31 to April 2. Dr Michael Palladino chaired the Andrology Laboratory Workshop. This full-day “Sperm Morphology Workshop,” held on April 2, was a laboratory-based class with hands-on training in the microscopic assessment of sperm morphology according to classification methods currently used in clinical laboratories. The program for the 30th Annual Meeting with the theme “Androgens and their Target Organs” featured 6 plenary lectures, 1 plenary debate, and 5 symposia. The meeting opened with the ASA Lecture “Genes, Gender, and Germ Cells,” presented by David Page, PhD, from the Whitehead Institute, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Boston. In an outstanding career spanning over 20 years, Dr Page's studies have addressed and answered fundamental questions concerning the mechanisms that underpin gonadal sexual differentiation. His work has been instrumental in elucidating the contribution of genes on the Y chromosome to male development, while illustrating potential mechanisms by which this chromosome has evolved to its current form in the human. His ASA Keynote Lecture described recent work in his laboratory that addresses the absence of information about how an ovary develops in the absence of a stimulus to become a testis. He points out that although it is clear that the somatic cell lineage, specifically the pre-Sertoli cells in the fetal gonad, drive formation of the testis, little to no information is available about how an ovary forms. As his tale of the 3 PhD students (Menke, Baltus, and Koubova) unfolded, we learned what happened when the team posed the hypothesis that the germ cells were the driver of somatic differentiation in the ovary. In an effort to identify genes involved in gender-specific gonad development, a subtractive hybridization experiment yielded predominantly somatic and male-specific genes, a disappointing blow to the original hypothesis. However, in reevaluation of the published gender-specific expression of the retinoic acid receptor-responsive gene, Stra8, Page's team learned that this gene was both female- and germ cell-specific in the fetal gonad, being expressed in accordance with the onset of meiotic prophase and directly preceding expression of other meiotic markers. A similar pattern was seen in the postnatal male germ cells, and additional experiments demonstrated that fetal expression of Stra8 correlated with germ cell differentiation into the female lineage, regardless of somatic and germ cell genotype. Production of a Stra8-/-mouse resulted in the cessation of germ cell development in both males and females coincident with meiotic onset, demonstrating the critical role of Stra8 in this stage of gametogenesis. To investigate this phenomenon further, organ culture experiments have illustrated the reliance of Stra8 expression on retinoic acid, and this can be manipulated in both male and female gonads, again illustrating the independence of this phenomenon from genotype. With additional culture data, Dr Page illustrated the potential importance of the P450 enzymes, which degrade retinoic acid, to suppression of Stra8 in the developing male gonad. The site and nature of the relevant enzymes remain to be determined, as does the manner in which these events affect somatic cell differentiation. The ASA Lecturer presented an elegant and convincing case for the importance of retinoic acid and germ cells as mediators of male gonad differentiation, and these studies provide the first demonstration of how the onset of meiosis is regulated in mammals. The International Lecture (ParentPlus Lecture) titled “Mutations in Male Infertility: Of Mice and Men” was given by Yoshitake Nishimune, MD, from Osaka University, Institute for Microbial Diseases, Osaka, Japan. ASA delegates were treated to an overview of the recent wide-ranging accomplishments of Dr Nishimune and his laboratory associates who are working to identify key genes involved in control of mammalian spermatogenesis. An estimated 25% of the mammalian genome is expressed specifically during the haploid phase of spermatogenic differentiation, and these are logical targets for fertility intervention and infertility investigations. Nishimune and colleagues set out to catalog these spermatid-specific genes in the mouse using a combination of cDNA expression library screening with spermatid-specific antibodies and cDNA subtractive hybridization studies. Dr Nishimune illustrated the identification and characterization of 80 genes, termed TISPs (transcripts increased in spermatogenesis). Many TISPs are characterized by the absence of introns (observed in 50%) and a TATA box, in addition to having an unusually high frequency of cyclic AMP response promoter elements (CREs) and being CpG rich. The derivation of knockout mice lines displaying male and female sterility has convincingly demonstrated their key roles in mammalian gametogenesis (DMC1, tektin-t, HANP1, TPAP, Prm1, Prm2). With the objective of understanding the contribution of gene mutations to the 60%-70% of cases in human infertility that are currently unexplained, Professor Nishimune and his colleagues began a search for single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) that were associated with human male infertility in a set of 226 fertile and 270 infertile patients. SNPs in 4 haploid genes (protamine 2, TNP1, haspin, and SCOT-t) were identified within the infertile sample set, and the effect of the DNA modifications was described and discussed. In several cases, SNPs were identified that were not associated with male infertility (TNP2, Prm1). Dr Nishimune stressed the need to continue screening a larger set of patients to understand the contribution of haploid-specific contributions to human fertility. On the same theme, Barbara Wakimoto, PhD, from the University of Washington presented “Toward a Comprehensive Genetic Analysis of Male Fertility Using Drosophila.” Drosophila melanogaster is a model organism that can be used to better understand the genetic basis of male infertility. Drosophila has several advantages, including well-characterized genetics and the availability of powerful tools, favorable cytology with the different developmental stages organized in chronological order in a single tube, and the presence of prototypical flagellated sperm. Dr Wakimoto presented an update on fertilization and paternal effect mutations that have resulted from a large-scale screen she and her colleagues have carried out in a search for male sterile mutations within the Zuker collection, a resource for the analysis of autosomal gene function in drosophila. Of over 2000 male sterile lines that were characterized, 81% failed during spermatogenesis, whereas 19% showed postspermatogenic abnormalities. Of the postspermatogenic sterile males, mutants were found that were defective in mating, sperm transfer, or storage and sperm-egg recognition. An interesting class of “paternal effect” mutants defective in sperm activation, pronuclear formation and competence, and paternal chromosome maintenance were of particular interest. Mutations in 5 different genes (eg, snky, a gene conserved in mouse and human) caused problems with plasma membrane breakdown. Characterization of the snky mutation suggested that the acrosome functions as a signaling vesicle rather than just a secretory vesicle in Drosophila, raising questions about conservation between species. Some mutants helped identify genetic pathways, such as those involved in acrosome biogenesis during spermiogenesis. Dr Wakimoto also described a reverse genetics technique, TILLING (targeting induced local lesions in genomes), she has been using more recently to uncover novel molecules involved in reproduction. In TILLING, one starts with a gene in which the mammalian homolog has a proposed or proven role in fertility and then looks for mutations in the gene in the Zuker collection. Dr Wakimoto expects this new high-throughput approach to facilitate the identification of multiple mutations within a given pathway. Given the conservation of cellular and molecular events between organisms, these efforts to identify factors that control male fertility in Drosophila should provide important information and insights for studies in humans. The Woman in Andrology Lecture on “Novel Glycolytic Enzymes and Sperm Motility” was delivered by Deborah O'Brien, PhD, University of North Carolina. Dr O'Brien's research has focused on this aspect of sperm biology. Previous research has shown that cytochrome C knockout mice are fertile, an unusual observation because this is the only cytochrome C source in sperm. Moreover, blocking oxidative phosphorylation does not impede fertility. Therefore, Dr O'Brien's work addresses the hypothesis that the glycolytic pathway is required for male fertility. Previous in vitro studies indicated that glycolysis is required for sperm hyperactivation and protein tyrosine phosphorylation, 2 events required for fertilization. Moreover, substances that are metabolized to (S)-3-chlorolactaldehyde, a glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate analog, are able to block fertilization. Interestingly, sperm glycolytic enzymes are located in the principal piece, not in the mitochondria, leading to the hypothesis that ATP is synthesized locally to support axoneme function and motility. Therefore, they isolated the mouse sperm fibrous sheath and conducted proteomic analysis to reveal a number of tightly bound glycolytic enzymes. Two enzymes are of particular interest: glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase-S (GAPDS) and phosphoglycerate kinase 2 (PGK2), because they are germ cell-specific and their inhibition blocks glycolytic ATP production. Sperm GAPDS (GAPD2 is the human ortholog), possesses a highly conserved, proline-rich N-terminus extension that is not present in somatic cell enzymes. The protein is expressed in late spermatids, although the mRNA is present much earlier during spermiogenesis. Proteolysis experiments indicate that this N-terminus is likely involved in GAPDS binding to the fibrous sheath and that this tight association is consistent with the hypothesis that GAPDS is important for sperm motility. GAPDS knockout mice were indeed infertile, although testis morphology, sperm production, and sperm structure appeared normal. Motility analysis, however, revealed that the sperm from the GAPDS knockouts was very poor (<0.1% progressively motile vs 61% for controls). As well, sperm proteins from the knockout mice were unable to undergo tyrosine phosphorylation as in controls. ATP production in these sperm was about 10% of the levels in control sperm, strongly suggesting that GAPDS is required for sperm ATP synthesis, which is required for motility and fertilization. Dr O'Brien's team also generated PGK2 knockout mice, and very recent data indicate these animals show severe male subfertility, although fertilization occasionally occurs. These mice also demonstrate a major defect in sperm motility, but to a slightly lesser degree than the GAPDS knockouts. Again, the PGK2 knockouts demonstrate low sperm ATP production (approximately 10% of control levels). Both of these germ cell-specific glycolytic enzymes are required for normal fertilization. The potential of these enzymes as contraceptive targets has also been broached with a structure-based design of inhibitors of sperm glycolysis. A recombinant form of GAPDS (without the proline-rich N-terminus region) was expressed, and homology models were generated. Inhibitor docking screening was then conducted to identify inhibitors that are predicted to fit into a functionally important pocket of GAPDS, according to the model. Taken together, this research provides great insight into the molecular mechanisms of sperm function and fertility and is pertinent to understanding certain causes of male infertility in addition to contraceptive development. The clinical lectures included Wayne Hellstrom, MD, Tulane University, who spoke on “Gene Therapy for Erectile Dysfunction.” Dr Hellstrom gave an enlightened and informative plenary lecture that began with a brief history of erectile dysfunction (ED) treatments, historically managed by sex therapists until the 1960s, when penile prosthesis surgery garnered the interest of urologists. He mentioned that the prevalence of ED is expected to increase over the next 30 years from the current 152 million men worldwide to an estimated 322 million men on the basis of current population trends. In speaking about the causes of ED, Dr Hellstrom reminded the audience that “erectile function is a monitor of the vascular system in general,” as conditions that affect the endothelium throughout the body such as diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemias likely also affect penile erections. Dr Hellstrom defined the need for more research into gene therapy strategies for ED because 30%-40% of men do not respond to currently available phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (PDE-5i). Possible indications for gene therapy in ED include patients who are PDE-5i nonresponders, cannot tolerate PDE-5i side effects, are not candidates for PDE-5i therapy, or are fearful of taking more oral medication. The advantages of gene therapy for ED could include restoration of complete function, no need for “planning” for sex that is currently required for PDE-5i's, reduction in use of concomitant oral therapies, and targeting therapy to specific abnormalities of erectile function. Six different approaches to ED gene therapy were then reviewed. Endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) gene therapy has undergone the most research, especially in diabetic and aging rodent models. Data from a working rodent model using an adenovirus vector to deliver eNOS intracorporally showed impressive responses in treated vs placebo (citrate) controls with minimal intracavernosal fibrosis or reaction. A second approach involves naked DNA transfer of maxi-K+ channel sensitizers that might reduce the stimulus needed for an erectile response. This therapy has been studied in aging and diabetic rodents and is currently undergoing phase I clinical trials in humans (data not available). A third approach attempts to reduce free radical and superoxide anion presence, molecules that bind with intracellular NO and reduce its availability for intracellular signaling during the erection process. Dr Hellstrom reported his findings from experiments in which adenovirus-mediated superoxide dismutase was transfected into diabetic rats to reduce reactive oxygen species with impressive responses. A fourth method of gene therapy for ED involves replacing important vascular growth factors, including VEGF and BDNF, that might restore function in arteriogenic and venogenic impotence. Manipulation of the RhoA/Rho kinase cascade upstream of the NO cascade is another approach to ED therapy. When activated, this pathway stimulates vascular constriction and might be responsible for why “men don't walk around with an erection.” If this cascade is inhibited, then smooth muscle relaxation and erections are possible. A double mutant model affecting this cascade was discussed. Last, Dr Hellstrom reviewed his recent work with mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) to treat ED. Injection of bone marrow-derived undifferentiated MSCs with and without adenovirus vectors and eNOS was discussed as potentially viable ways to restore normal endothelial function in corporal smooth muscle. Dr Hellstrom is very excited about the potential of these therapies and predicts that they will need a decade or so of further development before human treatments would become available. The American Urology Association Lecturer for 2005 was Ian Thompson, MD, University of Texas Health Sciences Center, San Antonio. He spoke on “Androgens and the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial.” Dr Thompson reviewed results of the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT), a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study to determine whether the 5-α-reductase type 2 inhibitor, finasteride, prevented prostate cancer in men at relatively low risk (with serum prostate-specific antigen [PSA] < 3 ng/mL). Follow up of men in the study was planned every 3 months for 7 years with an end-of-study prostate biopsy in all subjects. However, the PCPT was closed 15 months early because of a strong overall reduction in prostate cancer with finasteride treatment vs placebo, both in end-of-study biopsies and those done for cause (eg, elevated PSA). Further analysis revealed a reduction in low-grade (Gleason 5–6), but an increase in high-grade (Gleason 8–10), prostate cancer. A major controversy regarding the results of the PCPT is whether finasteride induced a real or artifactual increase in high-grade prostate cancer. Dr Thompson presented several lines of evidence that supported an artifactual rather than a real increase in high-grade prostate cancer with finasteride treatment: 1) In finasteride-treated men, the incidence of high-grade prostate cancer did not increase with time, as might be expected if finasteride increased the biological aggressiveness (and grade) of prostate cancer. 2) Androgen deprivation induced by an alternative method to finasteride (ie, gonadotropin-releasing hormone [GnRH] agonist treatment) resulted in a higher grade appearance of prostate cancer. 3) The proportion of Gleason 8–9 grade prostate cancers that showed degenerative changes was similar in finasteride- and placebo-treated men, arguing against an increase in tumor aggressiveness and grade induced by finasteride. 4) Gleason 7–10 grade prostate cancer was found bilaterally and in a larger percentage of cores (both measures of the disease extent within the prostate) more frequently in men treated with placebo than finasteride, and the pathological stage and positive margin rate was similar in finasteride- and placebo-treated men. 5) The percentage of men with high-grade prostate cancer was higher in finasteride-compared with placebo-treated men only in the end-of-study prostate biopsies, but not in the biopsies done for cause (eg, elevated PSA). title: The Polycomb group gene Ezh2 prevents hematopoietic stem cell exhaustion
abstract: The molecular mechanism responsible for a decline of stem cell functioning after replicative stress remains unknown. We used mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) to identify genes involved in the process of cellular aging. In proliferating and senescent MEFs one of the most differentially expressed transcripts was Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (Ezh2), a Polycomb group protein (PcG) involved in histone methylation and deacetylation. Retroviral overexpression of Ezh2 in MEFs resulted in bypassing of the senescence program. More importantly, whereas normal HSCs were rapidly exhausted after serial transplantations, overexpression of Ezh2 completely conserved long-term repopulating potential. Animals that were reconstituted with 3 times serially transplanted control bone marrow cells all died due to hematopoietic failure. In contrast, similarly transplanted Ezh2-overexpressing stem cells restored stem cell quality to normal levels. In a "genetic genomics" screen, we identified novel putative Ezh2 target or partner stem cell genes that are associated with chromatin modification. Our data suggest that stabilization of the chromatin structure preserves HSC potential after replicative stress.
authors: Leonie M. Kamminga; Leonid Bystrykh; Aletta de Boer; Sita Houwer; José Douma; Ellen Weersing; Bert Dontje; Gerald de Haan

title: Focus: Plant sciences in Korea
abstract: It sounded fresh and interesting when I was asked by Physiologia Plantarum to organize a ‘country-based’ focus issue. In addition to the journal's self interest, this type of special issue can reveal a country's scientific focus, which might not have been apparent even to the people involved in the research. An analysis of papers that have been published during last ten years in 36 plant-oriented scientific journals reveals a simple country-based sketch of global activity in the plant sciences (Table 1). Countries ranked within the top 10, in terms of the cumulative publication number, are mostly from Northern America, Europe, Japan and Australia. The cumulative number of papers from Asian countries, other than Japan, is much smaller than those from the leading countries but some have shown impressive increases in publication rates during this period. In particular, Korea and China have noticeably increased the number of papers being published annually, and in other parts of the world only Brazil equaled this increased output. Detailed analysis of how these countries have reinforced their scientific capability in plant biology, as well as other fields, is an interesting research topic and with this issue Physiologia Plantarum highlights the recent developments in experimental plant sciences in Korea. In this Focus Issue, we have invited fourteen articles, twelve review and two research articles, all written by Korean corresponding authors affiliated to Korean institutions, and we regret that we were not able to invite many other internationally well known Korean plant scientists to participate in this issue. This Focus Issue is not intended to focus on a specific topic, the aim is to highlight the achievement of Korean plant scientists working in diverse fields, and thus it necessarily contains a wide range of topics. However, for comprehensive understanding of the authors’ fields, the articles here are roughly grouped into five categories; growth and development, hormones and signaling, stress signaling, transport of macromolecules and Brassica genomics. The authors in this issue have worked for many years in their specialties, and this is reflected in the reviews published in this issue. In this section there are five reviews covering the topics of floral, leaf and root epidermal development, and expansin (the cell wall-loosening protein)-mediated plant growth and development. Two reviews by Noh and Noh (2006) and Lee et al. (2006) discuss the regulation of flowering time. The former review focuses on the role of chromatin modifiers and the latter emphasizes the cross-talk between signal integrators and the parallelism between Arabidopsis and rice in floral induction pathways. Multiple genetic pathways are operative to regulate the floral meristem identity genes for flower induction; namely, autonomous, vernalization, photoperiod, GA (gibberellin), and FRI (FRIGIDA) pathways (Boss et al. 2004; Putterill et al. 2004). Noh and Noh (2006) summarize the general role of chromatin remodeling tool kits in FRI, autonomous, vernalization, and photoperiodic pathways. FRI, autonomous, and vernalization pathways all targets FLC (FLOWERING LOCUS C, a floral repressor) transcription; negatively by FRI and positively by other two pathways. The review comprehensively illustrates that different sets of chromatin-remodeling factors, either directly or indirectly regulating histone methylation and acetylation, act on the FLC chromatin. The latest discoveries on the role of chromatin modifiers, such as BRAHMA, EBS, and TFL2, in the photoperiod pathway are introduced. The review by Lee et al. (2006) focuses on FT (FLORAL LOCUS T) as an integrator not only of the photoperiod pathway and the signal from FLC but also of the light-quality pathway and the signal directly (via FCA and FVE) from the autonomous pathway. The review integrates recent results demonstrating that signaling from CO (CONSTANS) to FT and SOC1 is not simply parallel but FT cross-talks to SOC1 to activate its transcription. The review highlights FT as a recently identified ‘mobile floral signal’(Huang et al. 2005), and discusses related topics and questions. Conservation and divergence of floral induction regulation in Arabidopsis and rice are described. The key components and integrators, such as FT, SOC1, and CO (HD3a, OsSOC1, and Hd1, respectively in rice), and the regulatory hierarchy between them in the pathways are well conserved in both species. However, the gear driven by Hd1 (rice CO) operates in reverse relative to the Arabidopsis counterpart so that Hd1 negatively regulates Hd3a (rice FT), consistent with the short-day property of rice floral induction. Another pathway through Ehd1, which positively regulates rice Hd3a and AP1, provides rice with its own floral induction pathway. Leaves, with their amazingly diverse forms, appear mostly as flattened two dimensional shapes. This may represent an adaptation for efficiently harvesting photons. However, plants invest considerable effort to keep this optimized shape. Among the characteristic mechanisms used by plants to achieve this are adaxial-abaxial polarity, proximal-distal polarity, polar expansion, symmetry, and flat morphology of the leaf. How these mechanisms operate together to produce a leaf is summarized by Kim and Cho (2006). The role of miRNAs during early leaf development was described. The review focuses on the polar expansion of the leaf; long and narrow vs. short and wide. Two pairs of genes, ROT3/AN and ROT4/AN3 for cell expansion and division, respectively, are shown to modulate this leaf property. The determination of cell fate is a fundamental process in the development of multicellular organisms, and thus understanding how this is governed has been on of the main challenges for developmental biology. Cells of the Arabidopsis root epidermis have two possible cell fates; hair cell or non-hair cell. The determination of these two fates is innately cell-position dependent and implemented by the interaction between MYB, bHLH, and WD40 proteins, where WEREWOLF (WER) and CAPRICE (CPC) for MYB transcription regulators, GRABRA3 (GL3) and ENHANCER OF GLABRA3 (EGL3) for bHLH transcription regulators, and TRANSPARENT TESTA GLABRA1 (TTG1) for the WD40 protein. The review by Schiefelbein and Lee (2006) provides an update on recent results demonstrating refined genetic interactions between these components and introduces a newly found factor responsible for positional information flow. Schiefelbein and Lee (2006) also focus on newly identified WER-binding cis-elements, the molecular genetic behavior of GL3/EGL3, and the proposed role of leucine-rich receptor like kinase SCRAMBLED (SCM), which could be a putative receptor of the positional cue from underlying root tissues. This review on root epidermal fate determination provides a well-illustrated model of regulatory circuits and flows from perception of the positional cue to cell specification. In this model, SCM perceives the positional signal and determines the positional expression of WER, and the downstream regulatory circuits ultimately control the expression of GLABRA2 (GL2), a repressor of hair morphogenesis. The review suggests several important future directions; for example, characterization of the relay molecules between SCM and WER, regulation of GL2 and GL3 by the MYBs, molecular function of TTG1, downstream molecules for hair morphogenesis and their regulation by GL2. Since the first two expansins, the cell wall-loosening proteins, were discovered in cucumber (McQueen-Mason et al. 1992), the expansin family has increased considerably, with 35 and 58 members found in the Arabidopsis and rice genomes, respectively. As the expansin family contains so many members, it has been divided into several subfamilies depending on amino acid sequence divergence and recently the nomenclature of these subfamilies has been unified; EXPA, EXPB, EXLA, and EXLB (Kende et al. 2004; http://www.bio.psu.edu/expansins/). A review by Choi et al. (2006) in this issue summarizes the evolution, expression, biochemistry, and biological function of this unique wall loosening protein family in different plant species. Among the interesting updates is the biochemical and biophysical properties of vegetative EXPBs, which bind tightly to cellulosic cell walls, in contrast to their soluble sister EXPBs from pollens. This review also refreshes the putative role of expansins in mycorrhizal activity and nodulation. A review on cytokinins by Hwang and Sakakibara (2006) focuses on the metabolism and perception of cytokinins. The metabolism section provides a helpful synthetic illustration of the different cytokinin metabolic pathways in higher plants and Agrobacterium. The difference in eukaryotic and prokaryotic pathways of cytokinin biosynthesis primarily appears to begin from the subtle difference in substrate specificities of isopentenyltransferases (IPTs, the first step catalyst) between the two systems; dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) in the plant cytosol and hydroxylated DMAPP in bacteria and plastids for the substrate. Seven Arabidopsis IPTs show different subcellular localizations and varying spatio-temporarily expression patterns, indicative of the ubiquitous role of cytokinins. Two AtIPTs are likely to have tRNA-IPT activities that produce cytokinins from tRNA by prenylation but their physiological role remains to be characterized. The review summarizes various ways of regulation of cytokinin metabolic enzymes. Among the major regulatory factors are hormones (auxin, abscisic acid, and cytokinin itself), developmental cues (SHOOT MERISTEMLESS, a KNOX1 protein), and nitrogenous compounds (NO3−, NH4+). The review provides a summary of verified cytokinin receptors and related histidine kinases. Intriguing phenotypic differences are described for the same AHK4/WOL/CRE1 allele. Diverse expression patterns and different molecular functions between the receptors are discussed so as to open new research directions in this field. Interestingly, among the many unpublished data mentioned in this review is the specified role of AHK3 in plant organ longevity. Lesions of AHK3, but not of AHK2 or AHK4, caused early senescence of the leaf, and its overexpression increased leaf longevity (Kim et al. 2006). Choe (2006) summarized recent advances in the research of brassinosteroid (BR) metabolism that is catalyzed mostly by cytochrome P450 monooxygenases. The review presents many parallels between BR biosynthetic pathways from different plant species. The final enzymes (and genes) in BR biosynthesis, from castasterone (CS) to brassinolide (BL), have been recently characterized from Arabidopsis and tomato (Kim et al. 2005; Nomura et al. 2005), and both steroids are also known to be biologically active in rice and pea. In this regard, an interesting interpretation was presented that BL may play a major role in reproductive development while CS is important in vegetative growth. This was inferred from the observations that tomato and Arabidopsis mutants defective in CS-to-BL conversion showed weak vegetative phenotypes. The second half of the review focuses on catabolism or inactivation of BRs. The degradation of these steroid hormones, balanced with their biosynthesis, is proposed as a mechanism to fine tune plant growth and development. Interestingly, it is suggested that agronomically advantageous phenotypes could be obtained through BR-deficiency; for example, short status, better photosynthetic capacity, more erect leaves, etc in cultivated rice. A research article by Joo et al. (2006) illustrates the cross talk between BR, auxin, ethylene, and light signaling networks. Ethylene biosynthetic enzymes, aminocyclopropane carboxylate (ACC) synthases, have long been known to be up-regulated by auxin. This paper provides further evidence that BR up-regulates ethylene production in dark-grown Arabidopsis seedlings, most likely by activating the expression of ACC synthase 4 (ACS4). However, light treatment or auxin-insensitive dominant mutations, such as axr1-3 and axr2-1, abolished the BR-induction of AtACS4, implying cross talk between BR, auxin, and light to regulate the ethylene level and thus to tune the seedling growth in different light conditions. Transport of macromolecules between cells is carried out either apoplastically or symplastically. Two reviews describe apoplastic sucrose transport and symplastic macromolecular transport. Sucrose loading from mesophyll cells to the phloem can be either apoplastic or symplastic. However, sucrose unloading in the developing seed is thought to occur apoplastically. To complete the apoplastic sucrose transport process, a three-protein (or enzyme) system is required; H+/sucrose transporter (SUT), invertase, and monosaccharide transporter (MST). Lim et al. (2006) summarized recent research on these proteins and genes from rice and other cereal caryopses. Functional studies of these genes in rice are expected from J-S Jeon's group as they have generated many T-DNA insertional rice mutants for these genes. There are many cases for non-cell autonomous action by certain genes. Transcription factors such as LEAFY, SHORTROOT, and KNOTTED1 (KN1) and other PD-transportable proteins are described together with the mechanism of how they pass through the PD channel. A recent interesting result by J-Y Kim's group is that the homeodomain of KN1 is not only necessary but also sufficient for PD trafficking (Kim et al. 2005). title: From genes to neurons to brain
abstract: Molecular biological approaches have played a key role in our growing understanding of nervous system function in health and disease. However, coupling individual molecular events with the function of distributed neural systems involved in complex behaviors and neuropsychiatric diseases requires the integration of reductionist molecular work with systems neuroscience. Genetic and genomic methods can help provide a systems context for individual molecular changes and also serve as a bridge between human biology and animal or cell models. For example, once genes are identified as causal or susceptibility factors in human disease, the appropriate use of animal or in vitro models will play a key role in clarifying the structural and functional changes occurring at the cellular and neural systems levels. In contrast, when the underlying circuits are well connected to a particular conserved cognitive function or behavior, work in the animal models to define the molecular etiologies can be appropriately translated to humans. With regard to both of these approaches, the manuscripts in this supplement that highlight several presentations from the advanced course ‘Genes and Neurons’ (held in July 2004 at the University of Minho, Braga, Portugal) share a common theme of bridging the gulf between genes and behavior. These papers reflect an area of research that is emerging as one of broad interest to the neuroscience community, as it represents recent advances that bridge the gap between genes, brain and behavior, in many cases using animal models to help shed light on complex human behaviors or cognition and disorders that affect these processes. This ‘Genes and Neurons’ supplement provides a broad overview of this area, covering both fundamental and hot topics, ranging from the basics of mouse behavior and cognition (Sousa, Almeida and Wotjak), genetic approaches to common psychiatric diseases (van Belzen and Heutink), to the MAP kinase (MapK) pathway in memory (Davis and Laroche), the genetics and neurobiology of mental retardation (MR) (Dierssen and Ramakers), the molecular basis of circadian behavior (Oster), a molecular systems level approach to anxiety (Stoppel, Albrecht, Pape and Stork), chromatin remodeling and developmental disorders (Santos and Maciel) and Alzheimer′ Dementia (Grazina and Oliveira). As such, this issue provides an extremely worthwhile and up to date review of these core topics in the molecular genetic basis of cognition and behavior for students and experts alike. In the comprehensively referenced ‘A hitchhiker's guide to behavioral analysis in laboratory rodents', Sousa and colleagues take on the difficult job of providing a template for approaching analysis of relevant behaviors in rats and mice. Several key points are worth noting. Sousa et al. emphasize the importance of using qualitative and quantitative strain differences in genetic mapping, and the challenges of moving from quantitative trait loci (QTLs) to genes, highlighting the development of more sophisticated and innovative analytic methods to facilitate these efforts. They focus on many critical practical issues that can impede proper assessment of behavior in mice, such as handling, training, stable routines and the failure to appreciate interstrain differences. Sousa et al. also appropriately caution us to be wary of over-interpreting molecular lesion studies, such as single-gene knockouts. Similar to anatomical lesion studies of the brain in developing animals, the functions being measured not only reflect the absence of a particular gene but also the potential consequences of environmental factors and molecular or behavioral systems' adaptations to the insult, including the use of alternative strategies not relevant to normal development or function. Lastly, they provide a practical guide for the general assessment of behavior, physical features and cognition in mice. It is clear from this extensive guide that although some of the areas such as motor behavior and memory are well established, several areas of particular relevance to human disease, for example, social behavior (of particular relevance to autism), are far less developed. Furthermore, how aberrancies in native social behaviors in mice correspond to human neurobehavioral disorders is a largely unexplored area. In a parallel introductory chapter, van Belzen and Heutink provide an exceptionally clear and thorough introduction on the use of modern genetic mapping tools to identify genes causing human psychiatric disorders. They move from explaining notions of heritability, the challenge of mapping complex disease genes and endophenotypes to providing concrete examples of approaches that have worked in defining genetic susceptibility factors in complex diseases, such as schizophrenia. Van Belzen and Heutink discuss linkage, association, candidate genes and issues of phenotype definition in a manner that is accessible to even the genetically unsophisticated audience, and as such this paper is highly recommended reading for those wanting a comprehensive introduction to this topic. They cite a number of advances in the genetics of psychiatric disorders, including work on Disc-1, Disbindin and other genes underlying genetic risk for schizophrenia that support their optimistic assessment of the outlook for the field of human psychiatric genetics. Here, the field has already made the jump successfully from humans to animal models in some cases. One of the neural circuits underlying complex behavior that has been extensively studied over the last two decades involves brain regions mediating fear and anxiety, which consist of highly conserved pathways that are very amenable to modeling in rodents. As Stoppel et al. note in their article ‘Genes and Neurons: Molecular Insight into Anxiety’, anxiety disorders and related conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), while having a heritable component in humans, are complex genetic conditions likely involving multiple genes interacting with the environment. Stoppel and colleagues appropriately champion the use of animal models, which allow molecular dissection of this circuitry, one gene at a time. They point out that studying these mouse models has allowed molecular dissection of molecules that modulate anxiety in the mouse, which has in turn clearly informed our understanding of human disease. In the case of fear conditioning, the knowledge of the behavior, circuitry and some initial molecular clues allowed for productive exploitation of this system in rodents to understand human anxiety in disease. QTL mapping in mouse has identified several loci that modulate distinct aspects of this process, and these loci can be compared with those identified in human conditions to help identify genes. Similarly, genes that modulate mouse behavior become candidates in studies of humans. This translational work is in its beginning, but the authors make it clear that the genes and systems already identified will be fruitful for understanding human genetic variation, perhaps related to PTSD and other debilitating neuropsychiatric disorders. Furthermore, because anxiety is such a prominent symptom in many human brain disorders, including dementia and developmental conditions such as Fragile X syndrome, better molecular targeting of this symptom domain is of great public health importance. The concept of MR as a phenotype driving genetic studies is controversial from the standpoint of modern cognitive neuroscience, which often emphasizes the study of discrete cognitive processes and the specific neural circuits that are their basis. However, from the standpoint of both public health impact and human genetics, MR syndromes are illustrative of success in multiple domains of the mouse model from gene identification and diagnostic testing to modeling. Dierssen and Ramakers highlight the phenomenon of dendritic pathology as a unifying feature across syndromes and across species. Such a neuropathological endophenotype is optimal for cross-species translation. These authors discuss the common pathology observed in MR as possibly affecting ‘communication systems’ in a global fashion across the brain. In this particular case, it is not clear precisely which anatomical or physiological substrates the authors are referring to by the terminology ‘communication systems.’ Perhaps, they mean to liken MR to a global disconnection syndrome involving higher order association areas, a concept that serves as one of the foundations of modern behavioral neurology (Catani & ffytche 2005; Geschwind 1965a, b). In this context, defects in axon pathfinding, neuronal migration or placement, synaptic plasticity and signaling properties of neurons all could lead to similar phenotypes, in which most primary sensory systems function, but carefully timed interregional communication of second-order and third-order association areas necessitated by most higher cognitive processes would be impeded. The authors discuss data from animal models of Down syndrome and Fragile X syndrome and in afflicted humans using functional imaging modalities that provide support for this disconnection hypothesis. Should such common processes be involved in rare and diverse forms of MR, it would provide potential for common treatment avenues in the future. In contrast to MR, memory function has been one of the topics explored most by modern cognitive neuroscience. Here, a huge literature on memory function in humans and animal models can be brought to bear on molecular genetic approaches. Homologous systems, from molecules, to regions, to specific forms of memory, have been identified across divergent species, including humans. Davis and Laroche review one of the hottest areas in the molecular basis of memory, the role of MapK signaling pathways in coupling synaptic signals to transcriptional changes that modify neuronal excitability at specific synapses. This is a confusing area to those outside the field, filled with a veritable alphabet soup; hence, although most of us wish to know more about MapK's, ras, rafs and Erks phosphorylate CREBs and other four letter words, this material is often hard to access at some basic, yet current level. Here, the authors not only explain what is known about this cascade in clear detail but also relate it to a wide variety of learning paradigms in model systems, from fear conditioning to object memory. Although the distinction between short-term and long-term memory has been clear at the psychological and anatomical level in primates and mice, the molecular basis of this distinction should be of particular interest for those outside of this rapidly moving field. One of the most interesting and highly conserved systems regulating complex human behavior is the circadian system, in which variation affects most of the other systems covered in this supplement, including memory, anxiety and social behavior. Henrik Oster reviews work in animal systems, including Drosophila, that have informed the study of human circadian behaviors at a molecular level. Oster contrasts the concepts of central vs. peripheral pacemakers, describing how both can be orchestrated in a hierarchical manner. Here, microarray studies have proven valuable, showing that nearly 10% of genes show circadian variability in expression. It is also important to note in the context of translation between animal models and humans that there is emerging data showing that this work has clearly informed human genetics and the molecular basis of sleep and circadian rythms in humans (Lowrey & Takahashi 2004; Xu et al. 2005). Two final papers address mechanisms of disease at the ends of the developmental spectrum, during early childhood and aging. Santos and Maciel review the role of the epigenetic regulation of gene expression in brain function and development. At a molecular level, epigenetic changes involve reversible but often heritable modifications that alter DNA function without changing actual DNA sequence. The role of epigenetics in neurodevelopmental disorders is emphasized by the role of imprinting in Prader–Willi/Angelman syndrome and dysregulation of a canonical form of epigenetic modulation, DNA methylation, in Rett Syndrome. In Rett syndrome, loss-of-function mutations in the global transcriptional regulator, MECP2, cause a striking, regressive and degenerative MR syndrome. Santos and Maciel critically analyze some of the unexpected results of classic microarray experiments performed on MECP2-null animals and provide a clear synthesis of the data on MECP2 targets that is moving to unravel the mystery of Rett pathophysiology. Furthermore, they review several studies that support their view that chromatin structure alterations are likely to play a role in a variety of cognitive and behavioral phenotypes in humans and provide a mechanism whereby environmental factors can have lasting effects on an individual genome and the genetic control of behavior. In the final paper of this supplement, Grazina et al. discuss their hypothesis-driven approach to unravel the genetics of a disease that has been challenging to model in rodents, Alzheimers Disease (AD). They provide an extensive summary of current literature on AD pathophysiology to highlight 12 potential biological pathways. In their synthesis, they elegantly couple an emerging literature on oxidative stress and the function of known Mendelian mutations to findings of energetic deficits in post-mortem AD brains, lending support to the hypothesis that mtDNA mutations may contribute to AD susceptibility. They describe a number of findings in case–control studies identifying potential pathophysiologically relevant changes in mtDNA, including one in the related disorder frontotemporal dementia. The data presented strongly support the biological plausibility of the mitochondrial hypothesis, and the authors provide one of the most scholarly analyses of all of the methodological and technical factors that may confound the results that I have seen. However, as they suggest, the absence of clear maternal inheritance, the non-replication of many findings, in what are mostly small case–control association studies, weakens the genetic support for this otherwise worthy hypothesis. In their critical assessment, the authors provide an ample roadmap for future research in this challenging but important area. The major unstated question looming over animal models of complex cognitive and behavioral human phenotypes is how much can we translate between these species that diverge at every level, from the complexity of cortical regions to single nucleotide polymorphisms. It is clear that even mouse and rat are quite distinct in many aspects of their behavior and brain organization. Yet, little has been done to directly address the relevance of mouse work to human cognition and behavior, presumably because of the complexity of such analyses. This is not to diminish the importance of models but to emphasize the necessity of analyzing data in the appropriate comparative and evolutionary context, so as to enable real progress in our understanding of brain dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disease. Such approaches necessitate development of new tools, and the application of systems biology approaches to permit a true synthetic view of human disease. The review articles included in this supplement were written by invited speakers from the course ”Genes and Neurons”, sponsored by the European Science Foundation, Functional Genomics Programme.
