title: The convergence of hematology and immunology (November 13–15; Tianjin, China)
abstract: The Convergence of Hematology and Immunology (CHI), which was sponsored by State Key Laboratory of Experimental Hematology, Institute of Hematology and Blood Diseases Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (CAMS), was held in Tianjin, China. Co-chaired by Tao Cheng of Institute of Hematology and Blood Diseases Hospital at CAMS (Tianjin, China), Lai Guan NG, and Florent Ginhoux of Singapore Immunology Network (Singapore), the two-day meeting invited 34 scientists from China, the United States, Singapore, Israel, Sweden, Switzerland, Japan, Italy, and Australia to present and share their latest views on the topics in hematology and immunology. This meeting has attracted more than 300 scientists and students. The highlights of the Convergence of Hematology and Immunology include keynote lectures, invited talks, and lighting talks selected from submitted abstracts. Another major milestone of this meeting was the announcement of the official opening of the Belt and Road Joint Laboratory. It would be impossible to highlight all the excellent speeches in this short report, but we hope to provide a glimpse of the topics discussed in the meeting. Prof. Sten Eirik Jacobsen of Karolinska Institute gave the first keynote speech focusing on the heterogeneity and lineage restriction within the hematopoietic stem cell compartment. After introducing previous single-cell transplantation studies, which uncovered considerable heterogeneity in lineage bias and restriction among reconstituting hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs), he suggested that such lineage bias or restriction might reflect generation of lineage-restricted unipotent or oligopotent self-renewing progenitors within the phenotypic HSC compartment. He next showed their published work, which uncovered a highly organized, predictable, and stable framework for lineage-restricted fates of long-term self-renewing HSCs following transplantation into myeloablated recipients. Single HSC transplantation and serial assessment of all blood lineages revealed limited and hierarchically related repertoire of adult LT-HSCs undergoing lineage-restricted fates. He emphasized that they identified the only single-lineage-restricted adult mouse HSCs (platelet-restricted), which adopted a fate toward effective and stable replenishment of a megakaryocyte/platelet lineage tree but not any other blood cell lineages, despite their sustained multipotency. Long-term genetic lineage tracing supports an important role of platelet-biased HSCs in unperturbed adult hematopoiesis. Platelet-biased HSCs expand upon aging. Until now, they found no evidence for lymphoid-biased LT-HSCs. Their work uncovers a limited repertoire of distinct HSC subsets, defined by a predictable and hierarchical propensity to adopt a fate toward replenishment of a restricted set of blood cell lineages following transplantation, before loss of self-renewal and multipotency. Prof. Paul Frenette of Albert Einstein College of Medicine gave the second keynote speech reviewing the work on hematopoietic microenvironment and aging of HSCs, as well as highlighting a novel “don’t eat me” pathway regulating acute myeloid leukemia clearance by phagocytes. It is well accepted that HSCs suffer a decline in their regenerative capacity and multi-lineage differentiation potential, leading to impaired immune responses and the development of hematologic malignancies. He showed that arterioles and megakaryocytes conferred specific microenvironments regulating functionally distinct subset of HSCs. Aging is associated with significant reductions in innervating adrenergic nerve fibers in the bone marrow. Denervation of the bone marrow of young mice produces all the hallmarks of HSC aging, including myeloid bias with lymphopenia and diminished repopulation capacity. Supplementation of a β3-adrenoreceptor agonist to old mice significantly rejuvenated the in vivo function of aged HSCs by acting on bone marrow stromal cells. Vascular cell adhesion molecule 1 (Vcam1) is an adhesion molecule expressed on macrophages, endothelial cells, and stromal cells. It mediates homing and retention of HSCs and progenitors into bone marrow. The recent studies by his group investigating the role of the macrophage niche in hematopoiesis revealed novel functions for Vcam1. They found that Vcam1 was also expressed on HSCs, and upregulated in human and mouse AML cases. High Vcam1 expression was associated with shorter survival. Further work demonstrated that Vcam1 played a role in the recognition of “self,” regulating AML progression via clearance inhibition by phagocytosis. Mononuclear phagocyte depletion prevented the clearance of Vcam1Δ/Δ AML cells. Hence, he suggested that targeting Vcam1 might represent a promising approach to eliminate leukemic stem cells in AML. Prof. Yasmine Belkaid of NIH gave the third keynote speech on the two interesting topics. First, how immune system adapts to transient nutritional stress. She showed that dietary restriction redirected memory T cells from secondary lymphoid organs to the bone marrow. This response is also accompanied by profound bone marrow compartment remodeling, erythropoiesis and adipogenesis. Prof. Belkaid also provided evidence to illustrate that enhanced T cell accumulation in the bone marrow was to preserve immunological memory during dietary stress. The other topic discussed was about how the host microbiota influenced immune responses. Specifically, she discussed about how microbiota affected the training of mucosal-associated invariant T cells (MAIT cells) at the early life exposure and would have a long-term impact on the development of immune response (protective during infection). This imprinting of MAIT cells is time sensitive, after this period MAIT cell development will be permanently impaired. Prof. Ido Amit of Weizmann Institute of Science gave the fourth keynote speech entitled “The power of ONE: immunology in the age of single cell genomics.” He highlighted single-cell genomics, which hold the potential to revolutionize the way we characterize complex immune cell assemblies through the study of their spatial organization, dynamics, clonal distribution, pathways, and crosstalk. He provided an overview of how recent single-cell genomic studies are changing the perspective of various immune-related pathologies from cancer to neurodegeneration. Following this, he introduced a technology called physical interacting cell sequencing, which would be a powerful tool to study interaction between two kinds of immune cells. First, the doublets, which contained two kinds of physically contacted immune cells, were sorted by FACS. Then the specific type of cells was separated from the doublets and sorted by FACS before they underwent single-cell sequencing. By using this technology, his group studied interactions between T cells and dendritic cells (DCs), showing that Tregs have high capacity to interact with DCs. Additionally, he also provided an overview of another novel technology called posttranslational modification sequencing, which coupled intracellular protein staining and single-cell sequencing technique. How this technique works is based on fixation, permeabilization, and RNA preservation of cells, followed by labeling with antibody against intracellular proteins and single-cell sequencing. Prof. Amit provided some of their preliminary data that revealed that MDSCs possessed unique signaling/metabolism activities such as ROS, iNOS, and ARG1. Prof. Chen Dong of Tsinghua University presented the works from his laboratory. He first showed from their genome-wide analysis, his group identified transcription factor NR4A1 was a key regulator for T cell activation. Their data showed that overexpression of NR4A1 inhibited T cell activation and differentiation and, on the contrary, deletion of NR4A1 broke T cell tolerance. Moreover, his group also identified transcription factor Tox2 that regulated differentiation of T follicular helper. Additionally, they also provided evidence to show that the Tox2-BCL6 axis formed the transcriptional network that was crucial for T follicular helper program. Prof. Jinyong Wang of Chinese Academy of Sciences brought the story about regeneration of transplantable T cell precursors from pluripotent stem cells by defined factors. His group established a new method to generate engraftable hematopoietic progenitors in vitro from pluripotent stem cells (iR9-PSC), which are capable of homing to thymus and developing into mature T (iT) cells in primary and secondary immunodeficient recipients. This differentiation is induced by synergistic and transient expression of Runx1 and Hoxa9 restricted in the time window of endothelial to hematopoietic transition and hematopoietic maturation stages. Notably, the iT cells distributed normally in central and peripheral lymphoid organs and exhibited abundant TCRαβ repertoire. The regenerative T lymphopoiesis rescued the immune surveillance ability in immunodeficient mice. Prof. Wang also presented data to show that gene-edited iR9-PSC produced tumor-specific-T cells in vivo that can effectively eradicate tumor cells. Collectively, their work provides insight into universal generation of functional and therapeutic T lymphopoiesis from the unlimited and editable PSC source. HSC transplantation is widely used in treatment of hematopoietic and nonhematopoietic disorders. However, how transplanted HSCs reconstitute hematopoiesis at the early stage after transplantation has not been elucidated due to technical limitations. Prof. Tao Cheng of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences gave a speech on rapid differentiation of transplanted hematopoietic stem cells revealed by single-cell transcriptomics. Based on single-cell RNA-sequencing datasets, his group identified 28 transcriptionally distinct subpopulations of hematopoietic cells. To understand the dynamic changes of transplanted HSCs in irradiated recipients, they tracked these cells within the first week after transplantation. Unexpectedly, the majority of the transplanted HSCs rapidly differentiated into multipotent progenitors. Occasionally, the HSCs gave rise to megakaryocytic/erythroid or myeloid precursors via a noncanonical differentiation path. Further work demonstrated that the cells arrived in the bone marrow from day 1 to day 7 progressively decreased the long-term reconstitution capability. This work uncovered the kinetics and fate choices of transplanted HSCs in myeloablated recipients at early stage and may have implications for clinical applications of HSCs and other stem cells. Macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells play crucial and distinct roles in tissue homeostasis and immunity. They also contribute to a broad spectrum of pathologies and are attractive therapeutic targets. Dr. Florent Ginhoux of Singapore Immunology Network reviewed their major work on dendritic cell and macrophage biology: from development to functions, providing deep insights of the origins and the mechanisms that govern their homeostasis and activation. In his talk, he first discussed about the origin of macrophages. He provided an overview of various data to show that macrophages arise from successive waves of embryonic and adult hematopoiesis, and that tissue resident macrophages in most tissues are established prenatally and self-maintained throughout adulthood. In adults, the origin of macrophages is heterogeneous. Monocyte-derived macrophages contribute to resident macrophages during adulthood but the kinetics and the degree of contribution varies among tissues. Subsequently, he discussed the heterogeneity of lung interstitial macrophages. By single-cell sequencing and transcriptomic analysis, two subpopulations, MHCII+ and MHCII− macrophages, were identified in lung interstitial macrophages. Further work demonstrated that the macrophage dichotomy was conserved across tissues. Moreover, two distinct interstitial macrophage subpopulations coexist across tissues in unique subcellular niches. He next showed that the Lyve1+ macrophages inhibited recruitment of inflammatory cells and fibrosis. During inflammation, adult-derived and embryonic-derived macrophages had different dynamics, that is, tissue-resident macrophages proliferate upon mild injury; both tissue-resident macrophages and monocyte-derived macrophages proliferate upon HSV skin infection and atherosclerosis; monocyte-derived macrophages proliferate upon severe inflammatory injuries. In the last part of his talk, he discussed about a molecule, Ms4a3, which was highly and specifically expressed in GMPs, GPs, and cMoPs but not in tissue-resident macrophage or DCs. Based on this information, they established several Ms4a3-based reporter mouse models, including Ms4a3TdT reporter, Ms4a3Cre-RosaTdT, and Ms4a3CreERT2-RosaTdT mouse models. Using these models, his group precisely quantified the contribution of monocytes to the tissue-resident macrophage pool during homeostasis and inflammation. The group of Prof. Bertie Göttgens of University of Cambridge has long been interested in deciphering the regulatory networks that control the development of blood cells in the embryo, homeostasis of the blood system in the adult, and how specific mutations can initiate system perturbations that ultimately lead to malignant transformation. In this meeting, he pointed out that cell atlas projects are important but descriptive. We need to find ways to address the mechanism leading to cellular decision-making in hematopoietic system. His group is undergoing multidisciplinary work combining single-cell molecular profiling, bioinformatics analysis, and experimental/functional validation to study the processes. He first reviewed advances in early organogenesis at single-cell resolution, such as scRNA-Seq atlas of mouse development from E6.5 to E8.5, new pipeline to access key regulatory genes by Chimera-Seq, defined molecular defect in cellular decision-making in Tal1−/−, new pathway involved in blood development, and validated Notch1 in Endo/Myocardium diversification. He then turned to their work in cellular decision-making in hematopoietic cells. By using a library containing 38 single-guided RNAs of transcription factors, his group screened 19 transcription factors important for lineage determination. These factors have many targets and formed complex interaction network, and they focused on two transcription factors, Ebf1 and Gata3, which are important for T/B lineage determination in progenitors. Prof. Timm Schroeder of ETH Zurich gave a talk entitled “Long-term single-cell quantification: new tools for old questions.” He pointed out the limitation of cell research, that is, we usually analyzed populations of cells rather than individual cells, and we take a “snapshot” view on a dynamic process. The immune system is a complex, dynamic, and plastic network composed of various interacting cell types that are constantly sensing and responding to environmental cues. Hence, his group developed imaging systems and software to image, segment, and track cells long term and to quantify divisional history, position, interaction, and protein expression or activity of all individual cells over many generations. These datasets were used for analyzing the dynamics, interplay, and functions of signaling pathway and transcription factor networks in controlling hematopoietic, pluripotent, skeletal, and neural stem cell fate decisions. HSCs are responsible for the life-long maintenance of blood production. In aging individuals, HSCs lose their regenerative capacity and show typical features of blood aging, including immunosenescence, anemia, and skewed myeloid cell production. The bone marrow HSC niche contributes in these processes. By using FACS, single-cell sequencing, and immunofluorescence, Prof. Emmanuelle Passegue of Columbia University discussed about the remodeling of the entire bone marrow niche microenvironment during aging process, such as remodeling of stromal compartment with the loss of endothelial compartment. In later part of her talk, Prof. Passegue touched on the role of cytokines in HSCs and progenitors. In particular, she mentioned TNFα and IL-1 signaling pathways in promoting aging in HSCs, which led to accumulation of poorly regenerative myeloid-biased old HSCs. After that, they provided evidence to show inhibition of IL-1 pathway with IL-1 antagonist in old mice in an improvement of old HSC regeneration upon 5-FU challenge. Lifestyle factors are well known to contribute to cardiovascular disease. Prof. Filip Swirski of Harvard University gave a talk on systemic inflammatory networks in cardiovascular disease. He focused on how lifestyle factors such as diet and sleep may impact on hematopoiesis and atherosclerosis. He presented how sleep can modulate CSF-1 production by pre-neutrophils to modulate monocyte production and atherosclerosis. Thus, this talk highlighted the importance of neuroimmune axis in modulation of hematopoiesis and disease outcome. Finally, the meeting ends with the final talk from Dr. Shachi Bhatt, the scientific editor of Journal of Experimental Medicine. She introduced the scope of the journal and the reviewing process of the journal, such as how the journal selects their referees, what the journal expects from the referees, how the editors make the decision based on referee's comments. This talk is especially useful for junior staff as it provides insights into the manuscript submission and review process of a top-tier journal. We also apologize to the many great speakers who attended this meeting but whose talks could not be discussed in this meeting report. These include Burkhard Becher of University of Zurich, Lee Grimes of Cincinnati Children's Hospital Medical Center, Bo Zhou of Shanghai Institute of Biochemistry and Cell Biology, Emery Bresnick of University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health, Jia Yu of Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences, Lai Guan Ng of Singapore Immunology Network, Jing Wang of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Chong Shu Zhen of Singapore Immunology Network, Scott Mueller of the University of Melbourne, Junke Zheng of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Matteo Iannacone of San Raffaele Scientific Institute, Hongbo Hu of Sichuan University, Ashley St. John of Duke-NUS, Hongbo Luo of Harvard University, Veronique Angeli of National University of Singapore, Naomi McGovern of University of Cambridge, Simon Yona of Hebrew University, Bing Su of Shanghai Institute of Immunology, Pengxu Qian of Zhejiang University, Satoshi Yamazaki of University of Tokyo, and Daniel Saban of Duke University who presented their work in hematology and immunology. The inaugural convergence of hematology and immunology meeting was a great success. Hematology and immunology are closely related research field. This was the first meeting allowing hematologists and immunologists around the world to discuss fundamental hematologic and immunologic questions and to share advances in both areas, which would help researchers in both areas to gain spark of thought leading to new ideas. The meeting also provided a chance for young scientists and graduate students in China to know advances in the field of both hematology and immunology from high-quality speeches, which would help them to gain deeper understanding of the two areas and have beneficial impact on their future career pathways.

title: Sex differences in mechanisms of disease
abstract: Nearly every known mental illness and neurological disorder afflicts both men and women, but very few affect them at equal rates. These discrepancies in disease prevalence suggest that biological sex may contribute to a person's risk and etiology of a given disorder, and therefore, understanding the influence of sex on disease mechanisms is critical for preclinical research. The articles in this issue—the second of two G2B Special Issues on sex differences—work toward this exact goal. Covering research in rodents and humans and topics ranging from maternal care, stress, substance abuse and Alzheimer's models, we offer a diverse look at the many ways in which sex, genetics and experience interact to shape brain health. Common to the emergence of many mental illnesses is exposure to stress, and sex differences in how stress impacts the brain likely contribute to sex-dependent outcomes in disease risk, symptoms and recovery. Two reviews on this topic lead the issue. First, Shaw et al1 examine one of the most stress-sensitive developmental periods, adolescence. They focus on the prefrontal cortex, which continues to mature throughout adolescence, undergoing critical windows of structural plasticity in both gray and white matter. That these key periods of synaptic pruning and myelination coincide with puberty provides a perfect opportunity for stress to elicit long-term, sexually divergent effects on brain structure, function and health. The authors pull from both human and rodent literature to describe the current state of evidence for these sex-dependent outcomes, drawing connections to the development of mental illness and neurological disorders. In the second review, Brivio et al2 take a brain-wide look at sexual dimorphism in stress-induced gene expression in both clinical populations and animal studies. They discuss the complex factors that can contribute to observed alterations in gene transcription, including stress modality, timing and experimental techniques used. They also provide exceptionally useful tables that outline acute and chronic stress effects on the expression of dozens of genes, broken down by animal sex and strain, brain region and type of stressor—a fantastic resource for our readers. Women are particularly susceptible to mood and anxiety disorders, and several research papers in this issue identify potential mechanisms underlying this imbalance. Kreutzmann et al3 report that previous exposure to foot shock stress improves safety learning in male mice, but not females, an effect that was dependent on neuropeptide S. In a new mouse model of stress-induced binge eating,4 females exhibited increased binging after a “frustration stress” experience, while poststress eating in males stayed constant. Stress can also lead to reinstatement of drug-seeking behavior, an effect observed equally in male and female mice. However, Lee et al5 show that the ability of the drug guanfacine to prevent stress-induced reinstatement of nicotine-seeking behavior in a conditioned place preference test depends on a novel interaction between sex and individual animals' preferred test chamber at baseline, suggesting a role for sex-dependent context processing in the likelihood of substance abuse treatments being successful. Other aspects of addiction—such as substance type, age of initiation, and abuse trajectories—have clear sex and gender differences, suggesting a need for sex-specific evaluation of addiction mechanisms. In a thoughtful review of both clinical and preclinical evidence, Datta et al6 argue that parallel genomic studies in human and model organisms represent a promising investigative strategy toward this end. Finally, a review by Booher et al7 explores the current literature on exercise as an ameliorative agent in animal models of alcohol use disorder. Although the vast majority of this work has been carried out only in male mice and rats, the studies that were conducted on both sexes suggest that exercise may be even more beneficial to females than it is in males. Two papers in this issue examine factors that can disrupt a behavior that is (at least in most laboratory rodents) uniquely female—maternal care—which can have long-lasting effects on offspring development and mental health. Reshetnikov et al8 find that prolonged separation from their pups during the first 2 weeks of life causes a robust decrease in pup licking, an effect accompanied by cell loss in the hippocampus and spatial memory deficits. Poor maternal care was also observed in mice with a double knockout (dKO) of two diacylglycerol kinase genes (eta and iota).9 dKO dams were deficient at pup retrieval and did not appear to feed their pups as often, resulting in only a 30% pup survival rate after postnatal day 3. These rodent papers are complemented by a review of the human literature connecting maternal caregiving behavior to DNA methylation in offspring.10 Notably, the authors include a discussion of the impact that maternal depression can have on epigenetic outcomes in children, especially in stress- and inflammation-related genes. Finally, two articles investigate potential sex differences in the 5xFAD mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (AD). AD is both more prevalent and more severe in women, but as in many fields, relevant preclinical research has been conducted primarily in male animals. Characterization of behavioral phenotypes in female genetic models will, therefore, be a critical step in determining their utility for understanding sex-dependent AD symptoms and disease trajectories. An extensive battery of locomotor behavior across the adult lifespan (age 3-16 months) showed that, despite robust motor deficits in 5xFAD mice of both sexes and a few age-dependent sex differences, very few sex × genotype interactions could be observed.11 Along similar lines, Grant et al12 found that whisking behavior in several exploratory tasks depended more on sex and the presence of retinal degeneration than on the 5xFAD genotype itself. Taken together, these studies suggest that this particular mutant may not be ideal for studying the aspects of AD that are sex-dependent. Collectively, the articles here show a clear need to consider sex a biological variable when investigating the molecular mechanisms that underlie disease symptomatology and treatments. We look forward to increased submissions to G2B in which data represent both male and female subjects, thus shedding a more balanced light on potential therapeutic targets for mental and neurological disorders.

title: LRP5 promotes adipose progenitor cell fitness and adipocyte insulin sensitivity
abstract: ABSTRACT WNT signalling is a developmental pathway which plays an important role in post-natal bone accrual. We have previously shown, that in addition to exhibiting extreme high bone mass, subjects with rare gain-of-function (GoF) mutations in the WNT co-receptor LRP5 also display increased lower-body fat mass. Here, we demonstrate using human physiological studies in GoF LRP5 mutation carriers and glucose uptake assays in LRP5 knockdown (KD) adipocytes that LRP5 promotes adipocyte insulin sensitivity. We also show that a low frequency missense variant in LRP5 shown to be associated with low heel bone mineral density in a genome wide association study meta-analysis, is associated with reduced leg fat mass. Finally, using genome wide transcriptomic analyses and in vitro functional studies in LRP5-KD adipose progenitors (APs) we demonstrate that LRP5 plays an essential role in maintaining AP fitness i.e. functional characteristics. Pharmacological activation of LRP5 signalling in adipose tissue provides a promising strategy to prevent the redistribution of adipose tissue and metabolic sequela associated with obesity and ageing.

title: RNF168-Mediated Ubiquitin Signaling Inhibits the Viability of BRCA1 -Null Cancers
abstract: Abstract BRCA1 gene mutations impair homologous recombination (HR) DNA repair, resulting in cellular senescence and embryonic lethality in mice. Therefore, BRCA1-deficient cancers require adaptations that prevent excessive genomic alterations from triggering cell death. RNF168-mediated ubiquitination of γH2AX at K13/15 (ub-H2AX) serves as a recruitment module for the localization of 53BP1 to DNA break sites. Here, we found multiple BRCA1-mutant cancer cell lines and primary tumors with low levels of RNF168 protein expression. Overexpression of ectopic RNF168 or a ub-H2AX fusion protein induced cell death and delayed BRCA1-mutant tumor formation. Cell death resulted from the recruitment of 53BP1 to DNA break sites and inhibition of DNA end resection. Strikingly, reintroduction of BRCA1 or 53BP1 depletion restored HR and rescued the ability of cells to maintain RNF168 and ub-H2AX overexpression. Thus, downregulation of RNF168 protein expression is a mechanism for providing BRCA1-null cancer cell lines with a residual level of HR that is essential for viability. Overall, our work identifies loss of RNF168 ubiquitin signaling as a proteomic alteration that supports BRCA1-mutant carcinogenesis. We propose that restoring RNF168-ub-H2AX signaling, potentially through inhibition of deubiquitinases, could represent a new therapeutic approach. Significance: This study explores the concept that homologous recombination DNA repair is not an all-or-nothing concept, but a spectrum, and that where a tumor stands on this spectrum may have therapeutic relevance. See related commentary by Wang and Wulf, p. 2720

title: Evaluating the Role of the Steroid and Xenobiotic Receptor (SXR/PXR) in PCB-153 Metabolism and Protection against Associated Adverse Effects during Perinatal and Chronic Exposure in Mice
abstract: BACKGROUND: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs) are environmental toxicants; PCB exposure has been associated with adverse effects on wildlife and humans. However, the mechanisms underlying these adverse effects are not fully understood. The steroid and xenobiotic receptor [SXR; also known as the pregnane X receptor (PXR) and formally known as NR1I2] is a nuclear hormone receptor that regulates inducible metabolism of drugs and xenobiotics and is activated or inhibited by various PCB congeners. OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to investigate the effects of exposure to PCB-153, the most prevalent PCB congener in human tissues, on SXR knockout mice (SXRKO) and to elucidate the role of SXR in PCB-153 metabolism and promotion of its harmful effects. METHODS: ) of PCB-153. Blood, livers, and spleens were analyzed using transcriptome sequencing (RNA-seq) and molecular techniques to investigate the impacts of exposure on metabolism, oxidative stress, and hematological parameters. RESULTS: SXRKO mice perinatally exposed to PCB-153 displayed elevated oxidative stress, symptoms of hemolytic anemia, and premature death. Transcriptomal analysis revealed that expression of genes involved in metabolic processes was altered in SXRKO mice. Elevated levels of the PCB-153 metabolite, 3-OH-PCB-153, were found in exposed SXRKO mice compared to exposed WT mice. Blood hemoglobin (HGB) levels were lower throughout the lifespan, and the occurrence of intestinal tumors was larger in SXRKO mice chronically exposed to PCB-153 compared to vehicle and WT controls. DISCUSSION: Our results suggest that altered metabolism induced by SXR loss of function resulted in the accumulation of hydroxylated metabolites upon exposure to PCB-153, leading to oxidative stress, hemolytic anemia, and tumor development in a mouse model. These results support a major role for SXR/PXR in protection against xenobiotic-induced oxidative stress by maintaining proper metabolism in response to PCB-153 exposure. This role of SXR could be generally applicable to other environmental toxicants as well as pharmaceutical drugs. https://doi.org/10.1289/EHP6262.

title: Cohort Profile: The Leipzig Research Center for Civilization Diseases–Heart Study (LIFE-Heart)
abstract: Coronary artery disease (CAD) is the most common cause of death worldwide and its prevalence is rapidly increasing in developing countries. CAD has a complex and heterogeneous aetiology involving numerous lifestyle, environmental and genetic factors whose interplay is only partly understood. Moreover, clinical presentation of the disease is highly heterogeneous, including subclinical asymptomatic forms, symptomatic stable disease of different severity, myocardial infarction and sequelae such as heart failure. Heritability of CAD is considerable, with estimates of ∼50%.1 Large-scale genome-wide association studies have discovered 168 loci associated with CAD as of now.2,3 However, little is known about the underlying biology at these loci. Moreover, studies were typically performed in a case/control setting often relying on anamnestic rather than physiological assessments of disease state. Efforts to analyse more refined phenotypes such as severity of disease, or sub-clinical phenotypes such as carotid plaques, are still in their infancy. The Leipzig Research Center for Civilization Diseases–Heart Study (LIFE-Heart, initially named the LE-Heart study) was set up to contribute to the understanding of the heterogeneity of CAD and the impact of molecular-genetic, lifestyle and environmental risk factors thereon. For this purpose, we aimed to establish a cohort with detailed vascular assessments. Severity of CAD was determined in (almost) all study participants by coronary angiography and atherosclerosis was assessed at different anatomical sites (e.g. carotid arteries). Concomitantly, we focused on comprehensive assessments of different molecular-genetic layers (genetics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics) in order to understand their inter-relationships and contributions to disease development. Our recruitment strategies enable us to define different disease entities and sub-groups with sufficiently large sample size to study potential molecular-genetic associations and biomarkers in and between these groups. As the genetic factors driving progression of CAD are an under-investigated issue, we continuously complete patient data from medical records and retrieve life status via registry offices. We also performed follow-up campaigns of mail-based questionnaires and reappointments for physical examinations. Based on the rich cross-sectional and longitudinal data and available biospecimens, our study is well suited to perform diagnostic and prognostic biomarker research to improve individual cardiovascular risk assessment and to develop personalized treatment concepts. LIFE-Heart is a monocentric study. All patients were recruited at the Heart Center Leipzig, Germany—one of the largest cardiology centers worldwide and with a catchment area covering several German states. The study was initially funded by the Roland-Ernst Foundation. LIFE-Heart is an integral part of the Leipzig Research Center for Civilization Diseases (LIFE), an organizational unit affiliated to the Medical Faculty of the University of Leipzig. LIFE is funded by means of the European Union, by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) and by funds of the Free State of Saxony within the framework of the excellence initiative. Follow-up investigations are again funded by the Roland-Ernst Foundation. In LIFE-Heart, three modes of patient recruitment were implemented. First, patients with suspected CAD as indicated by clinical signs or symptoms such as chest pain or ischaemia in exercise electrocardiogram were collected. Patients with previous coronary revascularization [percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)] or coronary artery bypass graft were excluded. Typically, these patients were admitted by their outpatient cardiologists to undergo diagnostic coronary angiography. A significant number of these patients showed no signs of occlusive CAD. Second, we enrolled patients with confirmed stable CAD, preferentially left-main CAD. Third, patients with myocardial infarction requiring PCI were collected either at emergency admission [acute myocardial infarction (AMI)] or after a myocardial infarction event (post-MI). General exclusion criteria included pregnancy, breast-feeding and severe systemic diseases such as auto-immune diseases treated with immune-modulating therapies, patients requiring dialysis, patients with acute or chronic infectious diseases and patients with cancer or cancer therapy within the last 2 years. Patients were recruited at hospital by randomly selecting consecutive patients fulfilling the respective inclusion criteria, with a maximum of three patients per day due to organizational restrictions. About 7300 patients were invited to participate. A total of 6994 patients (5025 male, 1969 female, age range 23–89 years) were successfully recruited. In 2018, we initiated a second follow-up campaign of patients without heart failure [left-ventricular ejection fraction ≥50%, N-terminal pro-brain natriuretic peptide (NT-pro-BNP) < 125 ng/ml]. Exclusion criteria include unstable CAD and cardiac valvular disease. Patients are re-invited and receive a physical examination comprising echocardiography, vascular status and laboratory tests with the major aim of detecting newly developed heart failure of different clinical appearance. Finally, in 2019 we started a mail-based follow-up campaign of all study participants to capture cardiovascular events since baseline, present complaints, changes in lifestyle and medication, nutrition, and, for the first time, gender aspects. Assessments are primarily focused on evaluating atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease states, related risk factors and sequelae. Coronary angiography is available for (almost) all patients at baseline including detailed evaluation of the degree of occlusion of coronary vessels allowing, for example, calculation of the Gensini score.6 Carotid vessels were assessed by high-resolution B-mode ultrasound images generated with the Vivid platform (GE-Healthcare, USA). We determined intima media thickness and plaque status of the common carotid artery, the carotid bulb, and the internal and the external carotid artery. Ankle–brachial index was determined by Doppler sonography sphygmomanometer cuffs and a hand-held Doppler probe (Huntleigh Mini-Dopplex, Germany). Patients were in a supine position and blood pressures were taken at both ankles and the right arm. In the follow-up, this method was replaced by automated photo-plethysmography (Vicorder, Skidmore Medical, UK). Additionally, we used Vicorder to perform pulse-wave analyses, deriving variables of vascular stiffness such as pulse-wave velocities between different anatomic sites.7 Electrocardiogram was determined at rest (5 min) and partly during exercise using a treadmill ergometer (LE 200 CE, CareFusion, Germany) or a semi-reclining cycle ergometer (Ergoselect 1000, ergoline GmbH, Germany). Transthoracic echocardiography was performed using again the Vivid platform (GE-Healthcare) with the following views: parasternal short and long axis, apical two, three and four chamber views, left and right ventricular outflow tract, tissue velocity imaging, spectral tissue Doppler, aortic, mitral, pulmonary and tricuspidal valve. Anthropometric assessments included height, weight and hip and waist circumference. In the follow-up, we added bio-impedance analysis using InBody 770 (JP Global Markets GmbH, Germany). Moreover, to assess sleep duration and physical activity, patients were asked to wear a Fit Bit Flex 2 (fitbit, USA) for 5 days combined with an activity protocol. Interview-based questionnaires comprise sociodemography, cardiac symptoms, complaints and events, medical history, medication, smoking behaviour, alcohol consumption and physical activity. In a subset of patients, the German version of the Food-Frequency-Questionnaire (FFQ) is available.8 In the follow-ups, we additionally ask for quality of life (SF-12), adherence to Mediterranean diet (MEDAS-149), anxiety and depression symptoms (HADS-D10) and gender roles (German version of the Personal Attributes Questionnaire11) An overview of available assessments per campaign can be found in Table 3. Overview of major assessments in each follow-up campaign Overview of major assessments in each follow-up campaign Besides follow-up campaigns, patient data are completed by linking medical records and continuously updating life status. Assessment of causes of deaths and linkage to records of insurance companies is in preparation. All assessments were performed following standard operating procedures (SOPs). Technical staff were regularly trained and supervised to comply with the SOPs. Data were captured by electronic data-entry systems and stored in a central database. A data quality and query management system was established. Standardized blood collection systems (Sarstedt, Germany; Becton Dickinson, USA) were used to collect the following biospecimens: serum, Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) plasma, citrate plasma, dried blood spots and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC). RNA of whole blood was stabilized using a PAXgene system (BD Bioscience, USA) later replaced by a Tempus system (Life Technologies, USA). Centrifugation of blood and PBMC samples was done between 30 and 60 min after blood collection. Samples were stored at 4 °C and transported within 5 h to the Institute of Laboratory Medicine of the University Hospital Leipzig (ILM) for laboratory analyses and storage. Aliquots of biospecimens were stored at −80°C or in the vapour phase of liquid nitrogen in the Central Biobank of the Medical Faculty of the University of Leipzig (Leipzig Medical Biobank). A comprehensive panel of blood analytes was assessed at the ILM on the day of blood sampling. The laboratory has been accredited according to the norms ISO 15189 and ISO 17025. Analyses were performed using automated Roche Cobas 6000/8000 clinical-chemistry analysers (Roche Diagnostics, Mannheim, Germany). The following variables were assessed: alanine aminotransferase, alkaline phosphatase, apolipoprotein A1 and B, aspartate aminotransferase, bilirubin, blood urea nitrogen, cholesterol, creatine kinase, creatine kinase MB, creatinine, high-sensitive C-reactive protein, gamma glutamyltransferase, glucose, haemoglobin A1c, HDL-cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, small-dense LDL-cholesterol, lipoprotein(a), NT-pro-brain natriuretic peptide, total protein, triglycerides, thyroid-stimulating hormone and high-sensitive troponin T (see Table 1). Differential blood counts were assessed using Sysmex XE/XN analysers (Sysmex, Germany). A special feature of LIFE-Heart is the comprehensive assessment of several multiomics layers including genetics, gene expression, proteome and metabolome at baseline. DNA was extracted from whole blood samples by Invisorb Spin Blood Maxi Kit (Invitek, Germany), dissolved in distilled water and stored at −80°C until analysis. Genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis was performed using Affymetrix-Axiom CEU or Affymetrix Axiom-CADLIFE micro-arrays. The CADLIFE array essentially contains the CEU array as a backbone accompanied by a custom content of SNPs near genes relevant for cardiovascular disease risk. RNA of whole blood was isolated using a PAXgene 96 Blood RNA Kit (QIAGEN/Becton Dickinson, USA) or Norgen Preserved Blood RNA Purification Kit I (Norgen Biotek, Canada). RNA from PBMC was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) and hybridized to Illumina HT-12 v4 expression micro-arrays (Illumina, USA). Proteome and metabolome analyses were based on liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) techniques developed at the ILM allowing high-throughput quantitative target assessment. title: Beta Human Papillomavirus and Merkel Cell Polyomavirus in Skin Neoplasms
abstract: Introduction In 1911, Peyton Rous from the Rockefeller Institute demonstrated that a transplantable, spontaneous, spindle cell sarcoma derived from a Plymouth Rock chicken could be virally transmitted to healthy chickens. This first known tumor virus was named Rous sarcoma virus. The discovery led to Peyton Rous being awarded the Nobel Prize in Medicine and Physiology in 1966 and to the recognition of a new paradigm in cancer research — virus-associated cancer. Since then, there has been growing interest in the role of viruses in cancer. By 1965, Tony Epstein, Yvonne Barr, and their colleagues had succeeded in establishing cell lines derived from Burkitt lymphomas and in visualizing herpesvirus-like particles, namely Epstein-Barr virus, as the first human virus linked to malignancy. Advanced molecular technology contributed to the identification of other human carcinogenic viruses such as hepatitis B virus, human papillomavirus (HPV), human T-lymphotropic virus-1, hepatitis C virus, Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus, and the most recently discovered Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) (Table 1). Most carcinogenic viruses establish persistent infections, typically occurring many years before malignancy. The viral genome is usually present in the tumor cells and is sometimes integrated into chromosomal DNA. These viruses are the etiologic agents for 15%–20% of all human tumors worldwide, and contribute to the carcinogenesis of diverse organs and tissues via central roles of cellular oncogene activation or tumor suppressor gene inactivation.1 The two milestones in skin tumor virology have come from the identification of the DNA viruses HPV and MCPyV, which have been isolated from nonmelanoma skin cancer (NMSC) and Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC), respectively.Table 1: Human tumorigenic viruses.The present review summarizes the current cellular and molecular evidence for the respective roles of beta HPV and MCPyV in the carcinogenesis of nonmelanoma squamous carcinoma and Merkel cell carcinoma, which are skin neoplasms originating from epithelium. HPV Etiology HPVs are small nonenveloped icosahedral viruses with double-stranded circular DNA genomes that infect the keratinocytes of skin and mucosa. Among the five major HPV genera (alpha-, beta-, gamma-, mu-, and nu-papillomavirus), the cutaneous HPV types associated with skin neoplasms are represented mainly by the beta genus, and are widely present in the skin of normal individuals.1 To date, more than 50 types of beta-HPV have been isolated, and the number is continuously growing (https://pave.niaid.nih.gov). Similar to the alpha-HPVs, beta-HPVs are divided into high-risk and low-risk types. Low-risk types such as HPV 1, 2, 3, and 4 are associated with verruca vulgaris, verruca plana, and verruca plantaris, while high-risk types such as HPV 5, 8, and 38 are thought to cause cutaneous malignancies. The present review will focus on these high-risk types. The beta-HPV genome is divided into a long control region and a coding region. The long control region contains the promoter, enhancer, and regulatory elements involved in viral DNA replication and transcription, while the coding region encodes the early (E) and late (L) proteins. The E proteins comprise E1, E2, E4, E6, and E7 (E5 is absent in beta-HPV types in contrast to the alpha genus) (Table 2); these are required for the regulation of viral gene expression and replication, and for the modulation of host cell protein function to create a cellular environment optimal for viral survival. The L proteins L1 and L2 are the major and minor capsid proteins, respectively, which are associated with the assemblage of viral structure (Fig. 1).2Table 2: Genome organization and encoded function of alpha- and beta-human papilloma viruses (HPVs).Figure 1: Genome of human papillomavirus (HPV) 38. HPV 38 is a member of the beta-HPV genus, and is represented by the black circle in the center of the figure. Three functional regions are displayed as different colors: the early region (E1–E7), the late region (L1–L2), and a long control region (LCR).To establish an infection, HPVs need to access the basal cell layer, which is normally protected by differentiated stratified epithelium. It is thought that the invasion is principally facilitated via micro-trauma in the epithelial barrier. However, beta-HPVs also target the hair follicle to maintain a persistent reservoir and initiate viral infection.3 HPV entry is generally deemed to occur via initial binding to heparan sulfate on the surface of basal cells and subsequent reaction with a specific secondary receptor; however, the definitive mechanism has not yet been fully clarified. Clinical implications Cutaneous HPVs are ubiquitous skin infections in the general population, and the tumors they cause are extremely rare in immunocompetent individuals. Beta-HPV genomes are likely etiologic agents of NMSCs that arise in immunosuppressed patients such as organ transplant recipients and human immunodeficiency virus-positive individuals, and are also detected in the tumor cells of patients with epidermodysplasia verruciformis (EV).3 The association between beta-HPVs and skin cancer was actually first reported in patients with EV, who frequently develop pityriasis versicolor-like lesions and large numbers of atypical, flat-topped, coalescing warts and subsequent invasive skin cancer such as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (CSCC), particularly in sun-exposed areas after 30–40 years.4 Compared with CSCC cases, the prevalence of beta-HPVs is higher in actinic keratosis, which is considered to be the precursor lesion of CSCC, suggesting that cutaneous HPVs may play a role in the early stage of skin carcinogenesis rather than in the maintenance of the malignant phenotype (the “hit-and-run” mechanism).5 Carcinogenesis A systematic review reported that beta-HPV infection may influence the associations between germline human leukocyte antigen variants and CSCC risk in immunocompromised patients by altering immune surveillance, DNA repair, and cell cycle progression, thus promoting clonal expansion of keratinocytes under ultraviolet radiation (UVR)-induced DNA damage.6 Most studies exploring the carcinogenesis of HPV have focused on high-risk HPVs from the alpha genus. However, more recent research has studied the role that beta-HPVs play in skin neoplasms, and how the beta E proteins may contribute to carcinogenetic pathways in similar or different ways to the alpha E proteins. In fact, unlike the alpha proteins that are integrated into the cellular genome, it seems increasingly likely that beta E6 and E7 are required only in the initial step of cutaneous carcinogenesis, but not in the maintenance of the tumor (the “hit-and-run” mechanism); this hypothesis was supported by a recent molecular study in a K14 HPV38 E6/E7 Tg mouse model.7 Oncogenic properties of beta-HPV E6 proteins Multiple studies have highlighted the potential carcinogenic activities of the E6 proteins of beta-HPVs by inhibiting the UVR-induced DNA damage repair mechanism and allowing keratinocytes with DNA mutations to survive and progress to carcinomas. Beta-HPV 5 and 8 E6s accumulate and disrupt the repairment of UVR-induced double-strand breaks by binding and attenuating p300 (a histone acetyltransferase) and thus diminishing the transcription of BRCA1/2 (two genes critical to the repair of double-strand breaks), ultimately curtailing the repair foci formation.8 It has been extensively shown that high-risk alpha-HPV E6 induces ubiquitination and degradation of the tumor suppressor protein p53 via binding to E6-associated protein (E6AP), a cellular protein with an E3 ubiquitin protein ligase function. However, the expression of E6 from beta-HPV types does not result in degradation of p53 in an E6AP-mediated manner. E6 of cutaneous HPV23 prevents p53 from phosphorylating on serine 46 by interfering with the ability of homeodomain-interacting protein kinase 2 to favor UVR-mediated apoptosis.9 In the presence of E6AP, beta-HPV E6 proteins drive the expression and activation of human telomerase reverse transcriptase (a catalytic subunit of the telomerase complex), which stabilizes the telomere length and improves cellular propagation and longevity in culture.10 In addition, the E6 proteins of beta-HPV types target the mitochondrial protein Bak for degradation, thus maintaining mitochondrial integrity and preventing UVR-induced apoptosis due to the interaction with E6AP.11 HPV5 E6 also recruits the HECT domain E3 ubiquitin ligase HERC1 to activate Bak for proteolysis in response to UVR-induced apoptosis.12 Combined with E6AP, E6 proteins of beta-HPV types stimulate and enhance Wnt signaling in Wnt-activated cells, thus promoting the stabilization, translocation, and accumulation of β-catenin in the nucleus; however, the E6 proteins of beta-HPV types play a smaller role in the potentiation of Wnt/β-catenin signaling than the E6 proteins of alpha-HPV types.13 Similar to the E6 proteins of alpha-HPVs, the E6 proteins of beta-HPVs mediate inactivation of p53 by interacting with the transcriptional co-activator CBP and p300. E6 of HPV5 and HPV8 inhibits phosphorylation of p300 by AKT, a serine/threonine kinase participating in the key role of the PI3K signaling pathway, resulting in its destabilization, which in turn leads to delayed ATR (ATM-Rad3-related protein, a member of PI3 kinase family) activation, and subsequently to reduced stabilization of p53, increased UVB-induced double-strand breaks, and accumulation of chromosomal abnormalities.14 Marthaler et al. identified CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha, a transcription factor regulating cellular differentiation, as a novel target of the HPV8 E6 protein via inducing p300 degradation, leading to the downregulation of miR-203 and upregulation of ΔNP63α protein, and eventually resulting in alteration of the cellular proliferation abilities.15 An additional mechanism of HPV E6-mediated skin carcinogenesis requires E6 binding to the transcriptional co-activator Mastermind-like protein 1 via its LXXLL motif; the downstream effect of this is an inhibition of Notch, which has a key role in keratinocyte differentiation and acts as a tumor suppressor in squamous epithelial cells.16 This mechanism is specific to the beta-HPVs, possibly as a consequence of their skin tropism. Aside from Mastermind-like protein 1, several Notch-associated components, including Notch1 and recombination signal binding protein for immunoglobulin kappa J region, are also found in complexes with the beta-HPV E6 proteins.17 Moreover, Mendoza et al. found that HPV5 E6 binds with Drosophila mothers against decapentaplegic protein 3 (SMAD3), a component in the transforming growth factor β1 signaling pathway, and thus represses SMAD3 transactivation by destabilizing the SMAD3/SMAD4 complex and mediating the degradation of both proteins.18 This biological response has also been observed in other beta-HPV types like HPV8, HPV17a, and HPV38,19-20 suggesting that the beta-HPVs are homogeneous to some extent with regard to their biology and the pathology of which binding partner or signaling pathway they are associated with. Oncogenic properties of beta-HPV E7 proteins HPV38 E7 proteins are involved in the stabilization of p53 by activating the transcription of ΔNp73, a dominant-negative isoform of p53 and p73, which inhibits the p53-regulated pathways to modulate the transcription of genes associated with growth suppression and apoptosis.21 In addition, E7 from HPV38 phosphorylates and accumulates ΔNp73α by inducing the translocation of Inhibitor of nuclear factor kappa-B (IκB) kinase beta in the nucleus.22 Moreover, HPV38 E7 oncoprotein promotes the formation of a multiprotein complex that includes ΔNp73α, IκB kinase beta, and two epigenetic enzymes (DNA methyltransferase 1 and enhancer of zeste homolog 2); this multiprotein complex specifically binds to several promoters of p53-regulated genes encoding proteins involved in DNA repair and apoptosis.23 The E7 oncoproteins from beta-HPV38 mediate the recruitment of the p53 antagonist ΔNp73α, which prevents the UVR-induced accumulation of the transcription factors p53 and c-Jun onto the Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) promoter; the resultant impairment of TLR9 gene expression plays a role in innate immunity and cellular stress response.24 Studies have shown that both the alpha and beta genera share common binding partners for E7 proteins to induce oncogenesis, suggesting that the related patterns of cellular pathway are highly conserved among diverse HPV types. The best-characterized function of E7 is the interaction mediated by its LXCXE motif with the pocket proteins retinoblastoma (pRb1) and the related proteins pRBL1 (p107) and pRBL2 (p130), resulting in the degradation of retinoblastoma protein (pRb), a tumor suppressor responsible for maintaining the cell in a quiescent state.25 Binding of E7 proteins from beta-HPV types (HPV38 and 49) to pRb leads to the phosphorylation of the latter, and to the release and activation of E2F1, which in turn induces the transcription of genes that are involved in cell-cycle progression.26 According to a systematic proteomic study, the other binding partners of HPV E7 proteins shared across the alpha and beta genera are Ubiquitin N-recognin Domain-Containing E3 Ligase 4 (p600), Potassium Channel Modulatory Factor 1, and Protein tyrosine phosphatase, Ubiquitin N-recognin Domain-Containing E3 Ligase 4 and Potassium Channel Modulatory Factor 1 are to be functional E3 ubiquitin with regard to the degradation of proteins. title: GWAS of epigenetic aging rates in blood reveals a critical role for TERT
abstract: DNA methylation age is an accurate biomarker of chronological age and predicts lifespan, but its underlying molecular mechanisms are unknown. In this genome-wide association study of 9907 individuals, we find gene variants mapping to five loci associated with intrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (IEAA) and gene variants in three loci associated with extrinsic epigenetic age acceleration (EEAA). Mendelian randomization analysis suggests causal influences of menarche and menopause on IEAA and lipoproteins on IEAA and EEAA. Variants associated with longer leukocyte telomere length (LTL) in the telomerase reverse transcriptase gene (TERT) paradoxically confer higher IEAA (P < 2.7 × 10−11). Causal modeling indicates TERT-specific and independent effects on LTL and IEAA. Experimental hTERT-expression in primary human fibroblasts engenders a linear increase in DNA methylation age with cell population doubling number. Together, these findings indicate a critical role for hTERT in regulating the epigenetic clock, in addition to its established role of compensating for cell replication-dependent telomere shortening.

title: Mechanisms of Lifespan Regulation by Calorie Restriction and Intermittent Fasting in Model Organisms
abstract: Genetic and pharmacological interventions have successfully extended healthspan and lifespan in animals, but their genetic interventions are not appropriate options for human applications and pharmacological intervention needs more solid clinical evidence. Consequently, dietary manipulations are the only practical and probable strategies to promote health and longevity in humans. Caloric restriction (CR), reduction of calorie intake to a level that does not compromise overall health, has been considered as being one of the most promising dietary interventions to extend lifespan in humans. Although it is straightforward, continuous reduction of calorie or food intake is not easy to practice in real lives of humans. Recently, fasting-related interventions such as intermittent fasting (IF) and time-restricted feeding (TRF) have emerged as alternatives of CR. Here, we review the history of CR and fasting-related strategies in animal models, discuss the molecular mechanisms underlying these interventions, and propose future directions that can fill the missing gaps in the current understanding of these dietary interventions. CR and fasting appear to extend lifespan by both partially overlapping common mechanisms such as the target of rapamycin (TOR) pathway and circadian clock, and distinct independent mechanisms that remain to be discovered. We propose that a systems approach combining global transcriptomic, metabolomic, and proteomic analyses followed by genetic perturbation studies targeting multiple candidate pathways will allow us to better understand how CR and fasting interact with each other to promote longevity.
authors: Dae‐Sung Hwangbo; Hye‐Yeon Lee; Leen Suleiman Abozaid; Kyung‐Jin Min

title: ZKSCAN3 counteracts cellular senescence by stabilizing heterochromatin
abstract: Zinc finger protein with KRAB and SCAN domains 3 (ZKSCAN3) has long been known as a master transcriptional repressor of autophagy. Here, we identify a novel role for ZKSCAN3 in alleviating senescence that is independent of its autophagy-related activity. Downregulation of ZKSCAN3 is observed in aged human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) and depletion of ZKSCAN3 accelerates senescence of these cells. Mechanistically, ZKSCAN3 maintains heterochromatin stability via interaction with heterochromatin-associated proteins and nuclear lamina proteins. Further study shows that ZKSCAN3 deficiency results in the detachment of genomic lamina-associated domains (LADs) from the nuclear lamina, loss of heterochromatin, a more accessible chromatin status and consequently, aberrant transcription of repetitive sequences. Overexpression of ZKSCAN3 not only rescues premature senescence phenotypes in ZKSCAN3-deficient hMSCs but also rejuvenates physiologically and pathologically senescent hMSCs. Together, these data reveal for the first time that ZKSCAN3 functions as an epigenetic modulator to maintain heterochromatin organization and thereby attenuate cellular senescence. Our findings establish a new functional link among ZKSCAN3, epigenetic regulation, and stem cell aging.

title: Dietary type 2 resistant starch improves systemic inflammation and intestinal permeability by modulating microbiota and metabolites in aged mice on high-fat diet
abstract: Type 2 resistant starch (RS2) is a fermentable dietary fiber conferring health benefits. We investigated the effects of RS2 on host, gut microbiota, and metabolites in aged mice on high-fat diet. In eighteen-month old mice randomly assigned to control, high-fat (HF), or high-fat+20% RS2 (HFRS) diet for 16 weeks, RS2 reversed the weight gain and hepatic steatosis induced by high-fat diet. Serum and fecal LPS, colonic IL-2 and hepatic IL-4 mRNA expressions decreased while colonic mucin 2 mRNA and protein expressions increased in the HFRS compared to the HF and the control group. 16s rRNA sequencing of fecal microbial DNA demonstrated that RS2 decreased the abundance of pathogen taxa associated with obesity, inflammation, and aging including Desulfovibrio (Proteobacteria phylum), Ruminiclostridium 9, Lachnoclostridium, Helicobacteria, Oscillibacter, Alistipes, Peptococcus, and Rikenella. Additionally, RS2 increased the colonic butyric acid by 2.6-fold while decreasing the isobutyric and isovaleric acid levels by half compared to the HF group. Functional analyses based on Clusters of Orthologous Groups showed that RS2 increased carbohydrate while decreasing amino acid metabolism. These findings demonstrate that RS2 can reverse weight gain, hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and increased intestinal permeability in aged mice on high-fat diet mediated by changes in gut microbiome and metabolites.

title: Dysfunctional telomeres trigger cellular senescence mediated by cyclic GMP-AMP synthase
abstract: Defective DNA damage response (DDR) signaling is a common mechanism that initiates and maintains the cellular senescence phenotype. Dysfunctional telomeres activate DDR signaling, genomic instability, and cellular senescence, but the links among these events remains unclear. Here, using an array of biochemical and imaging techniques, including a highly regulatable CRISPR/Cas9 strategy to induce DNA double strand breaks specifically in the telomeres, ChIP, telomere immunofluorescence, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), micronuclei imaging, and the telomere shortest length assay (TeSLA), we show that chromosome mis-segregation due to imperfect DDR signaling in response to dysfunctional telomeres creates a preponderance of chromatin fragments in the cytosol, which leads to a premature senescence phenotype. We found that this phenomenon is caused not by telomere shortening, but by cyclic GMP–AMP synthase (cGAS) recognizing cytosolic chromatin fragments and then activating the stimulator of interferon genes (STING) cytosolic DNA-sensing pathway and downstream interferon signaling. Significantly, genetic and pharmacological manipulation of cGAS not only attenuated immune signaling, but also prevented premature cellular senescence in response to dysfunctional telomeres. The findings of our study uncover a cellular intrinsic mechanism involving the cGAS-mediated cytosolic self-DNA–sensing pathway that initiates premature senescence independently of telomere shortening.

title: The NSD2/WHSC1/MMSET methyltransferase prevents cellular senescence‐associated epigenomic remodeling
abstract: Senescent cells may possess the intrinsic programs of metabolic and epigenomic remodeling, but the molecular mechanism remains to be clarified. Using an RNAi-based screen of chromatin regulators, we found that knockdown of the NSD2/WHSC1/MMSET methyltransferase induced cellular senescence that augmented mitochondrial mass and oxidative phosphorylation in primary human fibroblasts. Transcriptome analysis showed that loss of NSD2 downregulated the expression of cell cycle-related genes in a retinoblastoma protein (RB)-mediated manner. Chromatin immunoprecipitation analyses further revealed that NSD2 was enriched at the gene bodies of actively transcribed genes, including cell cycle-related genes, and that loss of NSD2 decreased the levels of histone H3 lysine 36 trimethylation (H3K36me3) at these gene loci. Consistent with these findings, oncogene-induced or replicative senescent cells showed reduced NSD2 expression together with lower H3K36me3 levels at NSD2-enriched genes. In addition, we found that NSD2 gene was upregulated by serum stimulation and required for the induction of cell cycle-related genes. Indeed, in both mouse and human tissues and human cancer cell lines, the expression levels of NSD2 were positively correlated with those of cell cycle-related genes. These data reveal that NSD2 plays a pivotal role in epigenomic maintenance and cell cycle control to prevent cellular senescence.

title: Deciphering the Mechanisms Behind Cardiovascular Disease: Long Noncoding RNAs as Key Molecular Signaling Hubs and Biomarkers of Atherosclerosis
abstract: Despite decennia of intense and active research, the etiology of complex diseases, such as those of the cardiovascular system (CVD), still remains to be fully understood and elucidated. At a fundamental level, risk factors can be classified as modifiable or nonmodifiable, with modifiable lifestyle factors such as physical activity along with nutrition being pivotal to the healthy maintenance and aging of the cardiovascular compartment. Moreover, exercise and diet have been recognized as key modalities in the primordial, primary, and secondary prevention of CVD, and combined with pharmacotherapy, in the tertiary management, rehabilitation, and treatment strategies of these conditions. Similar to most biological processes, those of the cardiometabolic systems are maintained in a state of dynamic and finely regulated equilibrium. This universal principle, identified by Claude Bernard in the 19th century, enables stability and survival in a constantly changing environment. It ascertains the relative homeostasis of major physiological parameters, such as body temperature, heart rate, hemodynamic blood flow, oxygen saturation of blood and tissue, pH, glucose levels, and blood pressure.1 Underpinning these vital parameters lies composite and exquisitely regulated molecular mechanisms and integrative biochemical interactions, systematized to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis. Although a considerable degree of redundancy and shift in the balance from the equilibrium point can be tolerated, even necessary for our physiological adaptive ability and providing a window for plasticity, excessive perturbations in major homeostatic bounds can have negative consequences, giving rise to chronic vascular inflammation, cellular dysfunction, and atherosclerosis (AS). Aberrant vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) and endothelial cell (EC) function is a sine qua non for the development and progression of CVD, which is characterized by a lag time between onset and clinical manifestation. This temporal deterioration of functionality exemplifies the attempted autoregulation of events that occur when the equilibrium of the CVD is disturbed, implicating the “causality” principles of CVD risk factors and the role of epigenetics in the etiology of AS. This results in altered patterns of gene expression over the course of time, at both the cell and tissue specific level. These modifiable and dynamic changes in the transcriptome are not dependent on changes in coding DNA sequence itself but on the epigenome. These epigenetic changes are defined by a collection of chemical marks on DNA and histones that controls chromatin architecture and associated regulatory binding proteins. It is established during embryogenic development and modified throughout our lifespan by age and lifestyle. In addition, this fine-tuning molecular mechanism of transcription is further complimented by posttranscriptional control of gene expression, also defined as an epigenetic mechanism, and combined together play an important role in the (patho-) physiology of many disease states, including CVD. In this issue of the Journal of Cardiovascular Pharmacology, Xie et al eloquently identified the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), LOXL1-AS1 as both a key molecular hub in the etiology of AS and a potential circulating diagnostic and/or prognostic biomarker. Technological advancements have enabled genomic and transcriptomic analysis with improved sensitivity and specificity. It has been elucidated that ncRNAs constitute approximately 98% of the transcriptome. Major strides in this new field in genomics have led to the identification and classification of different types of ncRNAs and quantification of their expression in different tissues and disease states. Deciphering the permutations and combinations of ncRNA expression profiles, along with advices in functional genomics, such as CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) and Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein-9) recombinant technology, with bioinformatic data analysis, has identifying ncRNA as key regulators of gene expression, fine-tuning biological processes, and homeostasis.2–4 In addition, growing evidence indicates that ncRNAs interact and coregulate each other. microRNAs (miRNAs) are evolutionarily conserved across species, emphasizing their many important functions. These diverse biological processes include cell cycle progression, proliferation, apoptosis, immunity, metabolism, and development. They are characterized as single-stranded ncRNAs of 17–27 nucleotides in length, fine-tuning gene expression by posttranscriptional silencing of specific target RNAs. Their effector function is elicited by a number of defined mechanisms. They may repress translation by mRNA targeting through their 5′ seed region (6–8 nucleotides). This in itself is not sufficient complementary nucleotide pairing to induce target mRNA cleavage but may interfere with the ribosome translational machinery. High compliment pairing between miRNAs and 3′ miRNA response elements located in the 3′UTR of target RNAs mediates RNA interference pathways through cleavage in the RNA-induced silencing complex. This combinatorial regulatory property of miRNA allows a single miRNA to have hundreds of different mRNA targets and a single gene transcript to be regulated by multiple miRNAs.5 lncRNAs are a class of RNA transcripts, more than 200 nucleotides in length, that lack any predicted coding sequence or ability. Nearly 60,000 human lncRNAs have been annotated to date and seem to exhibit strong tissue specificity, both in expression and functionality. Functional in vitro and model organism studies of the ever growing (l)ncRNA repertoire have demonstrated that they are involved in many biological pathways and (patho-)physiological processes at the epigenetic and transcriptional level. Therefore, defining the function of human lncRNAs will provide important insights into physiology and disease biology. lncRNAs act as molecular scaffolds for proteins interacting with transcription factors (TFs) or chromatin-modifying complexes to modulate gene transcription.3 In addition, lncRNAs may also act as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) whereby miRNAs and lncRNAs regulate each other through their biding sites.6 Interactions of miRNAs and lncRNAs have been reported to trigger degradation of the targeted lncRNAs and also to sequester miRNA, thus playing an important role in target gene expression. These interactions form complex, integrated and coregulatory networks, involving lncRNAs, miRNAs, small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), and PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to regulate gene expression. Xie et al present their findings and discuss the newly identified positive feedback loop between the lncRNA LOXL1-AS1, the miRNA miR515-5p, and the TF signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). This work is timely in that, in contrast to our expanding knowledge regarding the function of lncRNAs, the molecular intricacies regarding their mechanisms of action are largely unknown. Although protein-coding genes are largely conserved in mammals, the overwhelming majority of human lncRNAs is nonconserved and believed to be lineage specific. Although the low conservation of genomic sequences often suggests a limited or lack of function, emerging evidence supports that some nonconserved human lncRNAs clearly have functionality. The fact that some lncRNAs display structural but not sequence conservation emphasizes our lack of understanding of the mode of lncRNA conservation, making it challenging to elucidate lncRNA functionality and “modus operandi” in vivo. lncRNA LOXL1 antisense RNA 1 (lncRNA LOXL1-AS1) was first identified in the pathogenesis of the pseudoexfoliation (PEX) syndrome.7 Subsequently, it has been found to be an oncogenic lncRNA in many cancers, correlated with tumor size, distant metastasis, histological grade, and survival time. It regulates diverse cell functions, such as proliferation, cell cycle, migration, and invasion. Loss-of-function studies in osteosarcoma cell lines demonstrated knockdown of LOXL1-AS1 dramatically inhibited osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion through suppressing the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway.8 Mechanistically, LOXL1-AS1 acts through crosstalk and coregulation of various miRNAs and their associated signaling pathways. Xie et al found elevated levels of LOXL1-AS1 in the plasma of AS patients, highlighting its potential use as a CVD biomarker. Interestingly, in the context of CVD, LOXL1-AS1 expression has previously been demonstrated to be increased in response to both oxidative stress and cyclic mechanical stress in various human cell lines.9 Using in vitro techniques, Xie et al have identified LOXL1-AS1 as a functional lncRNA in both human VSMCs and ECs. Downregulation of LOXL1-AS1 was shown to inhibit proliferation and migration. This knockdown also promoted apoptosis in VSMCs and human umbilical vein ECs (HUVECs). Upregulation of LOXL1-AS1 was found to be through STAT3, a TF that mediates cellular responses to a variety of cytokines and growth factors. Both receptor and nonreceptor tyrosine kinases activate STAT3 by phosphorylation and dimerization. This is mediated through phosphorylation of JAK2, an intracellular nonreceptor tyrosine kinase. Dimerized STAT3 translocates to the nucleus, where it activates a variety of genes associated with cell growth, survival, and motility. Furthermore, LOXL1-AS1 was found to positively regulate STAT3 expression and was mainly distributed in the cytoplasm of VSMCs and HUVECs. This led Xie et al to hypothesize that LOXL1-AS1 regulates STAT3 expression through sponging miRNA, acting as a ceRNA. Through bioinformatic target prediction and molecular approaches, miR515-5p was identified and validated to bind with LOXL1-AS1 and STAT3 in VSMCs and HUVECs. In addition, LOXL1-AS1 could upregulate STAT3 expression by sequestering miR515-5p. A synopsis of the studies highlights are illustrated in Figure 1.FIGURE 1.: Diagram outlining the involvement of the lncRNA LOX1-AS1 in the etiology of AC. Increased expression levels of lncRNA LOX1-AS1 as a result of extrinsic risk factors, sequesters the miRNA miR515-5q by acting as a ceRNA. This results in a positive feedback loop, which facilitates EC and VSMC proliferation and migration, both hallmarks of AC (illustrated by R.P.M). JAK, Janus tyrosine kinase; NF-kB, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells; P, Phosphorylated; RISC, RNA-induced silencing complex; SRC, Src kinase family, non-receptor tyrosine kinases.This study highlights the potential role of ncRNAs as circulating functional biomarkers of CVD and maybe used to refine CVD diagnosis, treatment, and management strategies. Importantly, as key molecular hubs in CVD, developing novel therapeutics targeting ncRNA's involvement in AS has the potential to change the treatment landscape, facilitating more effective and targeted solutions. Although challenging to develop, they potentially will have applications for a wide range of diseases that are not effectively addressed with existing therapeutics.10

title: Genome-wide CRISPRi/a screens in human neurons link lysosomal failure to ferroptosis
abstract: Abstract Single-cell transcriptomics provide a systematic map of gene expression in different human cell types. The next challenge is to systematically understand cell-type specific gene function. The integration of CRISPR-based functional genomics and stem cell technology enables the scalable interrogation of gene function in differentiated human cells. Here, we present the first genomewide CRISPR interference and CRISPR activation screens in human neurons. We uncover pathways controlling neuronal response to chronic oxidative stress, which is implicated in neurodegenerative diseases. Unexpectedly, knockdown of the lysosomal protein prosaposin strongly sensitizes neurons, but not other cell types, to oxidative stress by triggering the formation of lipofuscin, a hallmark of aging, which traps iron, generating reactive oxygen species and triggering ferroptosis. We also determine transcriptomic changes in neurons following perturbation of genes linked to neurodegenerative diseases. To enable the systematic comparison of gene function across different human cell types, we establish a data commons named CRISPRbrain.

title: Genome-wide association studies identify 137 loci for DNA methylation biomarkers of ageing
abstract: Abstract Biological ageing estimators derived from DNA methylation (DNAm) data are heritable and correlate with morbidity and mortality. Leveraging DNAm and SNP data from >41,000 individuals, we identify 137 genome-wide significant loci (113 novel) from meta-analyses of four epigenetic clocks and epigenetic surrogate markers for granulocyte proportions and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1 levels, respectively. We report strong genetic correlations with longevity and lifestyle factors such as smoking, education, and obesity. Significant associations are observed in polygenic risk score analysis and to a lesser extent in Mendelian randomization analyses. This study illuminates the genetic architecture underlying epigenetic ageing and its shared genetic contributions with lifestyle factors and longevity.
